## Overview and reproducibility

This document compiles methodological details, supplementary analyses, and reproducibility outputs supporting the main manuscript.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}

It tests three preregistered hypotheses about the fungal community of willow ptarmigan dung across a seasonal contrast (winter, March vs. summer, June) replicated over three years (2022–2024):

-   **H1** — The dung fungal community differs in composition between the winter and summer timeblocks, and the magnitude of this seasonal shift is consistent across the three sampling years (2022–2024).
-   **H2** — Fungal alpha diversity is higher in summer than winter. On the diet-matched subset, per-sample fungal alpha diversity increases with per-sample dietary plant richness, consistent with diet acting as the dominant propagule source for the dung fungal community.
-   **H3** — On the diet-matched subset, individual fungal OTUs differ in *how specifically* they covary with the diet-plant community. Fungi tightly covarying with particular plant taxa are interpreted as likely ingested dietary passengers; taxonomically recognised coprophilous taxa (e.g. Sordariales) are expected to show diffuse, non-specific associations, consistent with their non-host-specific spore dispersal. Tight single-plant covariation is treated as the strong, interpretable signal.

Two exploratory aims accompany the preregistered hypotheses and are kept conceptually distinct from them:

-   **E1** — Identify fungal OTUs lacking a confident UNITE assignment that occur at non-trivial abundance ("dark taxa"); see Section 3.4.
-   **E2** — Document the occurrence and relative abundance of *Sporormiella*-type and other Sordariales taxa used in palynological reconstructions, to provide a modern avian reference point for a herbivore-presence proxy currently calibrated almost entirely on mammals; see Section 3.2. Note that E2 (a herbivore-presence proxy) is distinct from H3 (plant–fungus covariation) and from E1 (dark taxa).
:::

Computationally intensive steps (DADA2 denoising, LULU curation, iNEXT3D diversity estimation, GLLVM and Bayesian model fitting, phylogenetic community-structure null models) were executed on a remote Ubuntu-based computing environment. Their outputs (figures, tables, and selected model objects) are integrated here as static results, with the generating code shown in collapsible drop-downs in the HTML version.

All figures (PNG) and result tables (CSV) are stored within the project repository under `Supplementary/figures/` and `Supplementary/tables/` using relative paths. Rendering this document therefore requires cloning the repository and opening the `.qmd` file from the `Supplementary/` directory.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- project status; not part of the submitted appendix -->

## Status of this appendix

The analyses in **Sections 2–5** are finalized: they were regenerated end-to-end from the corrected canonical dataset and independently checked. **Section 6** (GLLVM, OTU-resolved H1) is integrated, with one flagged caveat — its fitted models predate the depth-filter correction (see the callout there). **Sections 7.1** (the Bayesian diet-richness mechanism for H2) and **7.2** (H3 OTU–plant covariation) are integrated. **Section 8** (functional guilds) is integrated and was regenerated from the corrected canonical dataset. **Section 9** (HMSC joint species distribution model) is integrated. **Section 10** collects the main-text figures and holds the authoritative build code for each; it is being populated as the main text is written.

**Correction of 2026-08-05 (affects a headline result).** The Section 4.2 PERMANOVA previously fitted `Year` as a numeric covariate rather than a factor, which tested only a linear trend across 2022–2024 and reported *no* Season × Year interaction. With `Year` correctly fitted as a factor the interaction is **significant** (R² = 0.10, p = 0.011): seasonal turnover is real and directionally consistent, but its magnitude differs among years. The Season main effect is unchanged. See the "Supersedes" note in Section 4.2, the new Table S5b, and Figure 2.
:::

## Section 1: Data and analysis objects {.unnumbered}

All downstream analyses draw on a small set of canonical phyloseq objects produced by `4_data_prep.R` and saved in `eco_analysis.RData` on the analysis server. Computationally intensive analyses were executed remotely; their outputs are stored under `tables/` and `figures/` and loaded/embedded as needed.

```{r load-objects}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true

load("eco_analysis.RData")  # produced by 4_data_prep.R

# alldat        : named list (nopool / pool / pspool). Primary analysis object.
#                 PCR replicates COLLAPSED by summing; non-fungal OTUs removed;
#                 taxonomy cleaned; depth filter >= 10,000 reads/sample.
#                 alldat$nopool = 52 samples (canonical object for PERMANOVA,
#                 iNEXT3D, dominance).
# alldat.rfy    : same as alldat but rarefied to the minimum depth (12,615 reads);
#                 used where even sampling effort is required (per-sample hillR).
# alldat_full   : one row per PCR replicate (never collapsed), pass-through depth
#                 threshold; for GLLVM / mixed-model work where PCR replicate is an
#                 explicit random effect (read-count offset, not rarefaction).
#
# The non-pooled (independent per-sample) DADA2 inference strategy ("nopool") is
# primary throughout, matching the numbered pipeline scripts.
```

## Section 2: Bioinformatics summary and study design

### 2.1 Study site and sampling design

Willow ptarmigan (*Lagopus lagopus*) faecal samples were collected at Lifjellet (Lierne municipality, Trøndelag, Norway) across a seasonal contrast: winter (March, snow-covered, browse-dominated diet) versus summer (June, green forage available) — replicated over three years (2022, 2023, 2024). The design is a Season × Year factorial, with repeated sampling of individually identifiable birds (microsatellite-confirmed where possible). Approximately 60 dung samples passed processing, of which \~31 have paired plant ITS2 diet data used for the H2 diet-richness mechanism (Section 7).

Each biological dung sample was amplified in two independent PCR replicates. DNA extraction, ITS2 amplification, demultiplexing (sabre), primer trimming (cutadapt), denoising (DADA2, non-pooled inference), and post-clustering curation (LULU) followed the workflow in `Scripts/1_demultiplexing.R`–`Scripts/3_taxonomic_assignment.R`; taxonomy was assigned against the UNITE reference (naïve Bayes, `minBoot = 80`). Negative, no-template, and extraction-blank controls were sequenced alongside samples and used for contaminant removal in `Scripts/4_data_prep.R`.

```{r tab-design}
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for the Season x Year design table"
library(knitr)
# Counted from the canonical per-sample table so the design cannot drift from the
# object every downstream analysis uses (52 samples, PCR replicates summed).
des <- read.csv("tables/guild_composition_per_sample.csv", check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(des) == 52, !anyNA(des$Season), !anyNA(des$Year))

tab <- table(factor(des$Season, levels = c("Winter", "Summer")), des$Year)
out <- cbind(as.data.frame.matrix(addmargins(tab, 2)))
names(out)[ncol(out)] <- "Total"
out <- cbind(Season = c("Winter (March)", "Summer (June)"), out)
out <- rbind(out, c("Total", colSums(out[, -1, drop = FALSE])))

kable(out, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(out) - 1)),
      caption = "Table S1. Season x Year sampling design of the final analysis set: biological dung samples retained after PCR-replicate collapsing, decontamination, non-fungal OTU removal and the 10,000-read depth filter. Each sample was amplified in two independent PCR replicates. Five of the 57 samples entering the depth filter were dropped by it (Figure S1, Table S2).")
```

### 2.2 Read and OTU tracking through the pipeline

This section reports read and OTU retention through each processing step for the primary `nopool` strategy.

```{r tab-tracking}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

trk <- read.csv("tables/report_read_otu_tracking.csv", check.names = FALSE)
trk <- trk[trk$strategy == "nopool", ]

step_labels <- c(
  "post_cutadapt_input_to_filter"            = "Post-cutadapt (input to DADA2 quality filter)",
  "post_quality_filter"                       = "Post quality filter (filterAndTrim)",
  "post_merge_denoise"                        = "Post denoise + merge pairs (pre-chimera ASVs)",
  "post_chimera_removal"                      = "Post chimera removal (ASVs)",
  "post_LULU_curation"                        = "Post LULU curation (OTUs)",
  "pcr_collapsed_decontaminated_taxassigned"  = "PCR replicates collapsed, decontaminated, taxonomy assigned",
  "non_fungal_OTU_removal"                    = "Post non-fungal OTU removal (PlutoF)",
  "depth_filter_final (>=10,000 reads)"       = "Final analysis set (depth filter >= 10,000 reads/sample)"
)

first_reads <- trk$total_reads[1]
trk_out <- data.frame(
  `Pipeline step`        = step_labels[as.character(trk$step)],
  `Samples / wells`      = trk$n_samples,
  `OTUs (ASVs)`          = ifelse(is.na(trk$n_taxa), "—", format(trk$n_taxa, big.mark = ",")),
  `Total reads`          = format(round(trk$total_reads), big.mark = ","),
  `% of starting reads`  = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * trk$total_reads / first_reads),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)

kable(trk_out,
      caption = "Table S2. Reads and OTUs retained at each processing step (nopool strategy).")
```

**Figure S1**: Per-sample sequencing depth after non-fungal OTU removal, before the depth filter (57 samples). Five samples (four winter, one summer) fall below the 10,000-read cutoff and are excluded from the analysis-ready dataset (52 samples).

![](figures/report_library_depth.png)

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code used to build the read/OTU tracking table and library-depth figure (report_prep_readtracking.R, executed on server)"

library(phyloseq)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# ---- Post-cutadapt / filter / merge / chimera / LULU counts, read from the
#      untouched script-2 workspace (nothing is rerun) --------------------------
e <- new.env(); load("merged_ITS.RData", envir = e)
out_df <- e$out_df
reads_postcutadapt <- sum(out_df$reads.in)
reads_postfilter   <- sum(out_df$reads.out)

dims_of <- function(m) data.frame(n_samples = nrow(m), n_taxa = ncol(m), total_reads = sum(m))

step_merge <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(step = "post_merge_denoise", strategy = "nopool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtab)),
  data.frame(step = "post_merge_denoise", strategy = "pool",   dims_of(e$merged_seqtabPP)),
  data.frame(step = "post_merge_denoise", strategy = "pspool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtabpsPP)))
step_chimera <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(step = "post_chimera_removal", strategy = "nopool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtab.nochim)),
  data.frame(step = "post_chimera_removal", strategy = "pool",   dims_of(e$merged_seqtabPP.nochim)),
  data.frame(step = "post_chimera_removal", strategy = "pspool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtabpsPP.nochim)))
step_lulu <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(step = "post_LULU_curation", strategy = "nopool", dims_of(e$nopool.lulu)),
  data.frame(step = "post_LULU_curation", strategy = "pool",   dims_of(e$pool.lulu)),
  data.frame(step = "post_LULU_curation", strategy = "pspool", dims_of(e$pspool.lulu)))

n_pcr_wells <- length(unique(sub("r[12]$", "", rownames(out_df))))
step_filter  <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("nopool","pool","pspool"), function(s)
  data.frame(step = "post_cutadapt_input_to_filter", strategy = s,
             n_samples = n_pcr_wells, n_taxa = NA, total_reads = reads_postcutadapt)))
step_qfilter <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("nopool","pool","pspool"), function(s)
  data.frame(step = "post_quality_filter", strategy = s,
             n_samples = n_pcr_wells, n_taxa = NA, total_reads = reads_postfilter)))

# ---- PCR-collapsed / decontaminated -> non-fungal removal -> depth filter,
#      from the freshly-regenerated comparison table (4_data_prep.R Section 8) --
cmp <- read.csv("phyloseq_comparison_summary.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cmp <- cmp[cmp$object %in% c("nopool","pool","pspool"), ]
relabel <- function(df, label) data.frame(step = label, strategy = df$object,
  n_samples = df$n_samples, n_taxa = df$n_taxa, total_reads = df$total_reads)

tracking <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  step_filter, step_qfilter, step_merge, step_chimera, step_lulu,
  relabel(cmp[cmp$step == "initial", ],             "pcr_collapsed_decontaminated_taxassigned"),
  relabel(cmp[cmp$step == "post_PlutoF_filter", ],  "non_fungal_OTU_removal"),
  relabel(cmp[cmp$step == "post_depth_filter", ],   "depth_filter_final (>=10,000 reads)"))
write.csv(tracking, "report_read_otu_tracking.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Library-depth figure: 57-sample post-non-fungal-removal depths, with the
#      10,000-read threshold and dropped samples marked --------------------------
load("eco_analysis.RData")  # nonfungal_ids_by_strategy, nopoolps.dada2
keep_taxa <- setdiff(taxa_names(nopoolps.dada2), nonfungal_ids_by_strategy$nopool)
ps_pp <- prune_taxa(keep_taxa, nopoolps.dada2)

depth_df <- data.frame(sample = sample_names(ps_pp), depth = sample_sums(ps_pp))
depth_df$Season <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps_pp))$Season
depth_df$status <- ifelse(depth_df$depth >= 10000, "kept (>= 10,000 reads)", "dropped (< 10,000 reads)")

ggplot(depth_df, aes(reorder(sample, depth), depth, fill = status)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10000, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("kept (>= 10,000 reads)" = "#4C72B0",
                               "dropped (< 10,000 reads)" = "#C44E52")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Reads per sample (log scale)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, size = 6),
        legend.position = "top")
```

### 3.1 Community composition across ranks

Per-sample relative read abundance at four taxonomic ranks, with samples grouped and ordered by Season (and Year).

**Figure S5**: Genus-level composition per sample, grouped by Season. Many summer bars are dominated end-to-end by a single genus (*Thelebolus*, *Sporormiella*, or *Coniochaeta*), consistent with the dominance analysis in Section 5, whereas winter bars are more evenly patchworked across genera.

### 3.2 Coprophilous (dung-specialist) genera (E2)

This subsection addresses exploratory aim **E2**: documenting the occurrence and relative abundance of *Sporormiella*-type and other Sordariales taxa used in palynological herbivore-presence reconstructions, to provide a modern avian reference point for a proxy currently calibrated almost entirely on mammalian dung.

The canonical tax table was screened against a standard list of coprophilous genera: *Sordaria, Podospora, Cercophora, Chaetomium, Schizothecium, Preussia, Sporormiella, Delitschia, Pilobolus, Ascobolus, Coprinopsis, Saccobolus, Sporormia*. Only ***Sporormiella*** (multiple OTUs) and a single trace ***Coprinopsis*** OTU were detected; none of the other genera appear in this dataset. Per-OTU winter/summer mean read shares and occurrences (number of samples per season, of 26 each) are shown below.

```{r tab-copro}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
copro <- read.csv("tables/report_coprophilous_by_season_v2.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(copro, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S3. Coprophilous-genus OTUs: mean read share (%) and occurrence per Season (canonical object, 52 samples; 26 winter / 26 summer).")
```

Total per-sample coprophilous read share is **higher in summer** than winter (Wilcoxon p = 0.006). Code for this table is shared with the dominance analysis and shown in Section 5.

### 3.4 Dark taxa and UNITE Species Hypothesis characterisation (E1)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- exploratory-status hedge -->

::: callout-warning
**Exploratory (E1); not yet definitive.** This subsection runs the authoritative UNITE `sh_matching` pipeline (v2.0.4, the service behind PlutoF) as a *complementary lens* on the taxonomically unresolved fraction of the community. It **does not modify the canonical taxonomy** used everywhere else in this appendix — Species Hypothesis (SH) matching and the DADA2/UNITE naïve-Bayes classifier answer different questions (which SH cluster and how novel, versus which confident Linnaean name) and are kept separate by design. Novelty calls and new-SH assignments here are preliminary and pending validation for the manuscript.
:::
:::

Nearly half of the retained fungal OTUs are **"dark taxa"**: 493 of 1129 (43.7%), accounting for 35.4% of reads that the naïve-Bayes classifier leaves without a confident genus. These are not spread evenly across the design: in the dominance analysis (Section 5.4), winter samples are markedly dark-taxa dominated, with dark taxa making up on average 51.3% of winter reads (a far smaller share in summer), and winter's single most persistent OTU (OTU1369) is itself a dark taxon. To make this unresolved winter community interpretable, every OTU's ITS2 sequence was matched against the UNITE SH reference set, which places each sequence into an existing species hypothesis or forms a new (candidate) one, independent of whether a Linnaean name is available.

```{r tab-e1-summary}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s <- read.csv("tables/E1_SH_assignment_summary.csv", check.names = FALSE)
e1_tab <- data.frame(
  Category = c("Dark OTUs (no confident genus)",
               " placeable to an existing named SH",
               " novel — forms a new species hypothesis",
               " no match to any UNITE SH (>20% divergent)",
               " excluded by ITSx (chimeric / non-ITS)"),
  `Dark OTUs` = c(s$n_dark, s$placeable_existing_SH, s$novel_new_SH,
                  s$no_SH_match, s$excluded_nonITS),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(e1_tab,
      caption = sprintf("Table S-E1a. UNITE Species Hypothesis placement of the dark-taxa OTUs (no confident genus in the canonical taxonomy). Median best-hit similarity to UNITE = %.2f%%; %d dark OTUs gained a finer lineage (family or deeper) from the SH consensus.", s$median_similarity, s$gained_finer_lineage))
```

**Most dark taxa are close to known references, and a live-database cross-check further shrinks the genuinely-novel fraction.** Against the local reference, of the 493 dark OTUs 143 were placeable to an existing named UNITE SH, 247 formed new (candidate) species hypotheses, and 90 had no SH match; 13 were dropped by ITSx. The novel and no-match sequences were then re-run through the PlutoF web service, whose reference database is larger and more current: this reclassified 79 formerly-novel OTUs across the community — 19 of them dark — as matches to existing named SHs (21 of the 79 resolving to species, and 11 of the 19 dark ones gaining a genus). Table S-E1a reflects this combined result: 162 placeable, 228 candidate-novel, 90 no-match. Each placeable OTU resolves to a stable SH page (`https://unite.ut.ee/sh/<code>`) carrying the taxon name and its DOI. The best-hit similarity distribution (Figure S-E1a) shows the dark fraction is bimodal — a spike near 100% (OTUs essentially identical to a reference but withheld a genus by the conservative `minBoot = 80` threshold) plus a real tail of divergent, candidate-novel lineages.

![](figures/E1_SH_similarity_hist.png)

**Figure S-E1a**: Best-hit similarity to the nearest UNITE Species Hypothesis, dark (no confident genus, red) versus named (grey) OTUs.

![](figures/E1_dark_taxa_novel_vs_placeable.png)

**Figure S-E1b**: Dark-taxa OTUs by SH placement category (placeable to an existing SH, novel/new SH, no SH match, or ITSx-excluded).

SH matching directly addresses the "winter = dark taxa" caveat: 34.6% of the winter dark-read burden is placeable to an existing UNITE SH, while the remainder forms candidate new SHs. Winter's dominant dark OTU, OTU1369, is genuinely novel: a candidate new SH only 85.4% similar to any reference, resolving no further than class Dothideomycetes.

**Toward permanent, citable identifiers.** Placeable taxa already carry citable UNITE SH identifiers (resolvable SH pages with DOIs). The candidate novel taxa are being registered: their representative ITS2 sequences are being deposited in a public archive (ENA) and imprinted as new SHs via PlutoF, which mints permanent DOIs — converting short-lived study detections into citable candidate species hypotheses (*registration in progress*; sequences in `models/E1_novel_taxa_for_plutof.fasta`).

```{r tab-e1-winter}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
w <- read.csv("tables/E1_winter_dominant_dark_taxa_SH.csv", check.names = FALSE)
w_disp <- w %>%
  transmute(
    OTU = OTU_ID,
    Class = sub("^c__", "", Class),
    `SH placement` = ifelse(!is.na(SH_URL), SH_code,
                     ifelse(SH_class == "novel_new_SH", "novel SH",
                     ifelse(SH_class == "no_SH_match", "no SH match", "excluded (ITSx)"))),
    `% id` = similarity_percentage,
    `Winter (n/26)` = paste0(winter_occ, "/", winter_n),
    `Winter %` = round(100 * winter_mean_share, 1),
    `Summer %` = round(100 * summer_mean_share, 1)) %>%
  head(12)
kable(w_disp, digits = 1,
      caption = "Table S-E1b. Top winter-abundant dark taxa and their UNITE SH placement. 'Winter %'/'Summer %' = mean per-sample read share within each season (26 samples each). Placeable SH codes resolve at https://unite.ut.ee/sh/<code>.")
```

(ii) On the PlutoF re-run, a reference-coverage heuristic flagged 248 of the resubmitted OTUs as putatively chimeric, but the *same* sequences passed cleanly in the local run and the flagged set is not the most-divergent one (median \~97% identity), so this flag is recorded (`plutof_chimera_flag`) but treated as unreliable and **not** used to exclude OTUs, pending scrutiny.

## Section 4: Community composition — H1 {.page-break-before}

H1 predicts seasonal compositional turnover of the dung mycobiome that is reproducible across years. Ordination and tests use **robust Aitchison distance** on the canonical depth-filtered object (`alldat$nopool`, 52 samples). Four complementary analyses are reported: an unconstrained PCoA (visualization), a PERMANOVA with beta-dispersion check (Season × Year), a per-year breakdown of the seasonal contrast, and a distance-to-Season-centroid linear model (does within-season heterogeneity itself depend on year?).

### 4.1 Ordination

![](figures/PCoA_Aitchison_Season_canonical.png)

**Figure S6**: PCoA on robust Aitchison distances (unconstrained), canonical object, coloured by Season and shaped by Year. Crosses mark Season centroids; thin segments connect each sample to its Season centroid.

This is the same ordination as main-text **Fig. 2A** (Section 10.2).

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Reading the axis percentages.** The percentages on the PCoA axes are far larger than is usual for a microbiome ordination, and they must not be read as "the plot captures 89% of the community variation". They follow from how `vegan` constructs robust Aitchison distances. `decostand(x, "rclr")` treats zero counts as missing rather than as observed zeros and, whenever any are present — always true of an OTU table — completes the matrix with a **rank-3 OptSpace approximation** (`vegan:::.calc_rclr`, argument `ropt = 3`). The robust CLR matrix from which the distance is computed therefore has rank 3 *by construction*, and the resulting PCoA has exactly three non-zero eigenvalues rather than the 51 that 52 samples would otherwise allow. PCoA1 and PCoA2 take 58.0% and 31.3% of that three-dimensional reconstruction and PCoA3 the remaining 10.7%, so the two plotted axes cover most of a space that had already been truncated to three dimensions before the ordination began. The same table under a full-rank Aitchison distance (CLR after a pseudocount) gives the ordinary figures instead: 13.7% and 9.5%, or 23.2% for the two axes together. **The percentages describe the display, not an effect size.** Every inferential statement about H1 comes from the PERMANOVA of Section 4.2, and none of it depends on them.

**Why 58% on the first axis and 11% for Season are not in conflict.** The axis percentages and the PERMANOVA R² of Section 4.2 are computed from the same distance matrix and the same total inertia, but they answer different questions and are not comparable as effect sizes. A principal coordinate is *fitted* to absorb as much variance as possible along a single direction, with no reference to any grouping, and is therefore the largest share obtainable; Season is a fixed, externally specified two-group split, which has no reason to align with that direction. Decomposed axis by axis, Season accounts for 15.3% of the variance along PCoA1, 4.0% along PCoA2 and 10.3% along PCoA3 — that is 8.9%, 1.2% and 1.1% of the total, summing to the 11.2% that `adonis2()` reports for the Season term. A dominant first axis that is mostly *not* seasonal is the expected result rather than a contradiction: most of what separates these samples is something other than season.
:::

### 4.2 PERMANOVA and beta-dispersion

```{r tab-permanova}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
perm <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova.csv", check.names = FALSE)
perm <- perm[, c("term", "Df", "SumOfSqs", "R2", "F", "Pr(>F)")]
names(perm) <- c("Term", "Df", "SumOfSqs", "R2", "F", "Pr(>F)")
kable(perm, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S5. PERMANOVA (adonis2) on robust Aitchison distances, Season x Year, by terms. Year is fitted as a FACTOR (2 df), so the interaction tests genuine year-to-year differences in the seasonal contrast rather than a linear trend across the three years.")
```

Because the Season × Year term is significant, the seasonal contrast is also tested separately within each year:

```{r tab-permanova-by-year}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
py <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova_by_year.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Year               = py$Year,
  `n (W/S)`          = paste0(py$n_winter, "/", py$n_summer),
  `R²`               = round(py$R2, 3),
  F                  = round(py$F, 2),
  `p`                = py$p_value,
  `Centroid distance`= round(py$centroid_distance, 1),
  `Spread W`         = round(py$dispersion_winter, 1),
  `Spread S`         = round(py$dispersion_summer, 1),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S5b. Season effect tested within each year separately (PERMANOVA on robust Aitchison distances). 'Centroid distance' is the Euclidean distance between the winter and summer centroids in robust-CLR space that year — the magnitude of the seasonal shift. 'Spread' is the mean distance to the cell's own centroid.")
```

```{r tab-betadisper}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
bd <- read.csv("tables/report_betadisper.csv", check.names = FALSE)
bd <- bd[bd$term == "Groups", c("grouping", "Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq", "F", "Pr(>F)")]
names(bd) <- c("Grouping", "Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq", "F", "Pr(>F)")
kable(bd, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S6. Beta-dispersion (permutest of distance-to-centroid homogeneity) for Season and Year.")
```

### 4.3 Distance-to-Season-centroid (consistency across years)

```{r tab-centroid}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cen <- read.csv("tables/report_centroid_lm.csv", check.names = FALSE)
cen <- cen[cen$term != "Residuals", ]
names(cen) <- c("Term", "Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq", "F value", "Pr(>F)")
kable(cen, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S7. Linear model of each sample's distance to its Season centroid (robust CLR space) ~ Season * Year.")
```

Main-text **Fig. 2B** (Section 10.2) plots the distances behind this table, split by Season and Year; it reads its p-values from `tables/report_centroid_lm.csv`, so the figure and Table S7 are guaranteed to agree.

::: {.callout-note when-profile="docs" appearance="minimal"}
**H1 interpretation — the two clauses separate.** Season is a significant predictor of community composition (PERMANOVA R² = 0.11, F = 6.92, p = 0.002), so the **first clause of H1 (seasonal turnover exists) is supported**. The **second clause (magnitude consistent across years) is not**: the Season × Year interaction is significant and substantial (R² = 0.10, F = 3.20, p = 0.011), meaning the size of the seasonal contrast genuinely differs between years.

Table S5b localises that interaction. The seasonal shift is strong in **2023** (R² = 0.24, p = 0.005; between-season centroid distance 35.7), much weaker in **2024** (R² = 0.14, p = 0.127; distance 10.3) and effectively absent in **2022** (R² = 0.02, p = 0.789; distance 6.9) — though this last figure is the one part of the breakdown that is sensitive to the distance measure, see caveat (iii) below. The *direction* of the shift is the same in all three years — it is the *magnitude* that varies, dominated by an unusually well-separated 2023. This is exactly the pattern the functional-guild analysis finds independently (Section 8.3: dung-saprotroph share summer versus winter is significant in 2023, marginal in 2024 and not significant in 2022).

The interaction is a difference in *location*, not merely in spread: the distance-to-Season-centroid model (Table S7) finds a strong Season effect on within-season spread (p \< 0.001) but **no** Season × Year interaction in that spread (p = 0.79). In other words, summer communities are consistently more heterogeneous than winter ones in every year, while how far apart the two seasons sit changes from year to year.

**Caveats.** (i) Beta-dispersion is significantly higher for summer than winter samples (F = 15.3, p = 0.002; Table S6), so part of the PERMANOVA R² reflects this difference in within-group spread rather than a pure centroid shift (Anderson 2001); this previews Section 5's finding that summer communities are individually more dominance-skewed. (ii) With three years and 15–19 samples per year, a single atypical year moves the interaction substantially; the per-year tests in Table S5b are correspondingly low-powered (no year has more than 10 samples per season). The safe reading is *"seasonal turnover is real and directionally consistent, but its magnitude is not established as constant across years"* rather than a positive claim about year-specific ecology.

(iii) The distance itself carries an assumption, and one specific claim above depends on it. As set out in Section 4.1, `vegan`'s robust Aitchison distance is computed from a rank-3 completion of the robust CLR matrix, so this PERMANOVA — like the ordination — is run on a three-dimensional reconstruction of the community rather than on its full dimensionality. Refitting the identical `Season * Year` model on full-rank distances gives the same qualitative verdict with smaller effect sizes:

```{r tab-permanova-sens}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
sn <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova_sensitivity.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Distance            = sn$distance,
  Rank                = sn$rank,
  `Season R²`         = round(sn$season_R2, 3),
  `Season p`          = sn$season_p,
  `Year R²`           = round(sn$year_R2, 3),
  `Year p`            = sn$year_p,
  `Season × Year R²`  = round(sn$interaction_R2, 3),
  `Season × Year p`   = sn$interaction_p,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S7b. Sensitivity of the H1 PERMANOVA to the distance measure. All four rows are adonis2(d ~ Season * Year, by = 'terms') on the same canonical 52-sample object, 999 permutations, seed 20260805. 'Rank' is the number of non-negligible positive eigenvalues the distance admits: robust Aitchison is capped at 3 by vegan's rclr completion, the others are full-rank. The first row is the one reported in Table S5.")
```

The per-year breakdown is exposed to the same choice, and more sharply:

```{r tab-permanova-sens-year}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
library(knitr); library(tidyr)
sy <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova_sensitivity_by_year.csv", check.names = FALSE)
sy$cell <- sprintf("%.3f (p = %.3f)", sy$R2, sy$p_value)
wide <- pivot_wider(sy[, c("distance", "Year", "cell")], names_from = Year, values_from = cell)
names(wide)[1] <- "Distance"
kable(wide, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S7c. Season effect within each year, under each distance measure (R² with permutation p). Same models as Table S5b, refitted on each distance. The robust-Aitchison row is the identical test to Table S5b; its p-values differ in the third decimal (0.775 / 0.009 / 0.116 here against 0.789 / 0.005 / 0.127 there) only because each cell here is seeded independently, so the two draw different permutation sets. R² values are exact and match.")
```

Both H1 verdicts are robust to the choice of distance — Season is significant at p ≤ 0.002 under every measure and the Season × Year interaction at p ≤ 0.011 — but the reported R² values sit at the optimistic end of their range: the Season term is better read as 0.07–0.11 and the interaction as 0.05–0.10 rather than as precise variance shares. The Year main effect is the one term whose *significance* changes (p = 0.309 under robust Aitchison, p = 0.004–0.027 under the full-rank measures), which is a further reason not to lean on it.

**One statement in this section needs qualifying.** The per-year breakdown's finding that 2022 shows essentially no seasonal shift (R² = 0.02, p = 0.789) is an artefact of the rank-3 distance. Under all three full-rank measures the 2022 contrast is modest but unambiguously present (R² = 0.09–0.10, p ≤ 0.010; Table S7c). What survives every distance is the *ordering* — 2023 strongest (R² = 0.21–0.24), then 2024, then 2022 — and it is the size of the gap, not its direction, that the rank-3 distance exaggerates. The defensible reading is that the seasonal shift occurred in **all three years and was largest in 2023**, rather than that it was absent in 2022. Section 8.3's independent guild result should be read the same way: it shares this ranking, but its non-significant 2022 cell is a question of power, not of a missing effect.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- records a correction to an earlier draft -->

::: callout-important
**Supersedes.** Earlier versions of this section reported no Season × Year interaction (p ≈ 0.95). That came from an error in `working/report_prep_permanova.R`, where `Year` was passed to `adonis2()` straight from `sample_data()` and so entered the model as a **numeric covariate (1 df)**, testing only a linear trend across 2022–2024 rather than the factorial interaction. `Year` is now fitted as a factor (2 df), as it always was in the distance-to-centroid model of Section 4.3. The Season main effect is essentially unchanged (R² = 0.112 in both); only the Year and Season × Year terms are affected. Corrected 2026-08-05; the same fix was applied to `Scripts/5_community_composition.R`, whose PERMANOVA is print-only.
:::
:::
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code used to generate the PCoA, PERMANOVA, beta-dispersion, and centroid tables (report_prep_permanova.R, executed on server)"

library(phyloseq); library(vegan); library(ggplot2); library(dplyr)
load("eco_analysis.RData")
ps <- alldat$nopool  # canonical, 52 samples, >= 10,000 reads

otu_mat <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)

# ---- Unconstrained PCoA on robust Aitchison distances ----
d_ait <- vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison")
attr(d_ait, "Labels") <- rownames(otu_mat)   # vegdist drops Labels for robust.aitchison
ord   <- capscale(d_ait ~ 1)
# NB: rank 3, not 51 -- vegan's rclr completes the matrix at rank 3 (Section 4.1),
# so these percentages are shares of a 3-D reconstruction, not of the full data.
eig   <- pmax(ord$CA$eig, 0)
ax1p  <- round(100 * eig[1] / sum(eig), 1); ax2p <- round(100 * eig[2] / sum(eig), 1)

sc <- as.data.frame(scores(ord, display = "sites", choices = 1:2, scaling = 1))
colnames(sc)[1:2] <- c("Axis1", "Axis2"); sc$sample <- rownames(sc)
meta_p <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps)); meta_p$sample <- rownames(meta_p)
sc$Season <- droplevels(factor(meta_p$Season[match(sc$sample, meta_p$sample)]))
sc$Year   <- droplevels(factor(meta_p$Year[match(sc$sample, meta_p$sample)]))
cent <- aggregate(cbind(Axis1, Axis2) ~ Season, sc, mean); names(cent) <- c("Season","cX","cY")
sc <- merge(sc, cent, by = "Season")

ggplot(sc, aes(Axis1, Axis2, colour = Season, shape = Year)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = cX, yend = cY), alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = cent, aes(cX, cY, colour = Season), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 3, shape = 4, stroke = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  xlab(paste0("PCoA1 (", ax1p, "%)")) + ylab(paste0("PCoA2 (", ax2p, "%)")) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

# ---- PERMANOVA + beta-dispersion (Season x Year) ----
sampledf <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))
dists <- vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison")
perm  <- adonis2(dists ~ Season * Year, by = "terms", data = sampledf)
write.csv(cbind(as.data.frame(perm), term = rownames(perm)), "report_permanova.csv", row.names = FALSE)

beta_s <- betadisper(dists, factor(sampledf$Season)); pt_s <- permutest(beta_s)
beta_y <- betadisper(dists, factor(sampledf$Year));   pt_y <- permutest(beta_y)
write.csv(dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(grouping = "Season", term = rownames(pt_s$tab), pt_s$tab, check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(grouping = "Year",   term = rownames(pt_y$tab), pt_y$tab, check.names = FALSE)),
  "report_betadisper.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Distance-to-Season-centroid (robust CLR space) ~ Season * Year ----
rclr <- decostand(otu_mat, "rclr", MARGIN = 1)
dimnames(rclr) <- dimnames(otu_mat)   # vegan's rclr imputation path drops dimnames
meta <- data.frame(sample_data(ps), check.names = FALSE)
centroids <- rowsum(rclr, meta$Season) / as.vector(table(meta$Season))
euclid <- function(x, y) sqrt(sum((x - y)^2))
meta$dist_centroid <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(rclr)),
  function(k) euclid(rclr[k, ], centroids[meta$Season[k], ]), numeric(1))
mod <- lm(dist_centroid ~ Season * Year, data = meta)
write.csv(cbind(term = rownames(anova(mod)), anova(mod)), "report_centroid_lm.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Section 5: Diversity — H2 {.page-break-before}

H2 predicts higher summer alpha diversity, tracking the richer summer diet. Two Hill-number approaches are presented together deliberately, because they appear to disagree in an informative way: coverage-based iNEXT3D (which pools samples within a Season and asks about the Season's total species pool) versus per-sample hillR (which asks about diversity within a single sample and rewards evenness). The disagreement is resolved by the dominance analysis in 5.3.

### 5.1 iNEXT3D: coverage-based taxonomic diversity

![](figures/H2_iNEXT_TD_by_Season.png)

**Figure S7**: iNEXT3D coverage-based rarefaction/extrapolation of taxonomic Hill numbers (q = 0, 1, 2), samples pooled within each Season (incidence data, nboot = 500). Summer exceeds winter at every q.

```{r tab-inext}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
inx <- read.csv("tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_asymptotic.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(inx, digits = 2,
      caption = "Table S8. iNEXT3D asymptotic taxonomic-diversity estimates by Season (Hill q = 0, 1, 2; observed and asymptotic, with s.e. and 95% CI).")
```

The asymptotic estimates in Table S8 are plotted as main-text **Fig. 3A** (Section 10.3).

### 5.2 Per-sample Hill diversity and mixed model

![](figures/H2_hill_boxplot_Season.png)

**Figure S8**: Per-sample Hill numbers (PCR-collapsed object, rarefied to the minimum sample depth). Summer \> winter at q0 (richness) but winter ≥ summer at q1/q2 (Shannon/Simpson) — a richness–evenness crossover.

This is the same quantity as main-text **Fig. 3B** (Section 10.3), which redraws it to the main-figure specification: annotated with the Table S9 contrasts below, and stacked beneath the pooled estimates of Fig. 3A on a shared set of facet columns. Figure S8 is retained here as the plain, unannotated view.

The Season main effect is tested with a frequentist mixed model fitted at the PCR-replicate level, with PCR replicate (and, where estimable, Year and individual bird) as random intercepts. The `re_structure` column records the random-effects structure that actually converged for each Hill order.

```{r tab-lmm}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
lmm <- read.csv("tables/H2_lmm_season_effect.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(lmm, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S9. Mixed-model Season effect (summer minus winter) on per-replicate Hill diversity, with 95% CI and p, for q = 0, 1, 2.")
```

### 5.3 Why the two metrics disagree: dominance and evenness

The crossover is not an artifact. iNEXT3D pools a Season's samples and rewards the total species list (summer's samples collectively contain more species, so summer wins at every q). Per-sample q1/q2 instead downweight rare taxa and reward *within-sample evenness* — and individual summer samples are far more dominance-skewed than winter ones, so a single summer sample's effective diversity is often lower even though its raw species list is longer.

```{r tab-dominance}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
dom <- read.csv("tables/report_dominance_summary.csv", check.names = FALSE)
names(dom) <- c("Season", "n", "Mean richness", "Mean top-1 OTU share (%)",
                "Mean Pielou J", "Wilcoxon p (richness)",
                "Wilcoxon p (top-1 share)", "Wilcoxon p (evenness J)")
kable(dom, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S10. Per-sample richness, top-1-OTU dominance, and Pielou evenness by Season, with Wilcoxon tests (canonical object, 52 samples).")
```

Concretely: a summer sample's single most abundant OTU accounts for **56%** of its reads on average (vs **25%** in winter, p \< 0.001), and Pielou evenness is correspondingly much lower (J = 0.38 summer vs 0.72 winter, p \< 0.001). Summer gains many rare taxa (the long tail iNEXT3D detects) on top of one or two OTUs that dominate the read count — richness rises, evenness collapses, and q1/q2 track evenness more than richness.

### 5.4 Which OTUs dominate each Season?

```{r tab-top5}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
top5 <- read.csv("tables/report_top5_otu_by_season.csv", check.names = FALSE)
clean_tax <- function(v) ifelse(is.na(v) | v == "", "—", sub("^[a-z]__", "", v))
top5$Season  <- tools::toTitleCase(top5$Season)
top5$Order   <- clean_tax(top5$Order)
top5$Genus   <- clean_tax(top5$Genus)
top5$Species <- clean_tax(top5$Species)
top5 <- top5[, c("Season", "OTU", "mean_pct_share", "Order", "Genus", "Species")]
names(top5) <- c("Season", "OTU", "Mean % share (within-season)", "Order", "Genus", "Species")
kable(top5, digits = 2,
      caption = "Table S11. Top-5 dominant OTUs per Season by mean within-season read share, with taxonomy.")
```

Summer's dominance is driven by three strongly season-skewed OTUs: **OTU1 (*Thelebolus*)** averages 24.9% of summer reads (15/26 summer samples vs 5/26 winter at 3.2%), **OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*)** is essentially summer-only (10.1% vs 0.2%), and **OTU636 (*Sporormiella* cf. *intermedia*)** is also summer-skewed (9.0% vs 2.5%). Winter's own top OTU, **OTU1369**, is a "dark taxon" (unclassified below Class, Dothideomycetes), present in 20/26 winter samples but only 3/26 summer, at 11.2% mean winter share.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for iNEXT3D + per-sample hillR + mixed model (report_prep_partA_diversity.R) and dominance/top-5/coprophilous (report_prep_dominance.R), executed on server"

## ---------- iNEXT3D coverage-based TD by Season ----------
library(phyloseq); library(iNEXT.3D); library(hillR)
library(lme4); library(lmerTest); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)
load("eco_analysis.RData")

ps  <- alldat$nopool
sd  <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps))
OTU <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (!taxa_are_rows(ps)) OTU <- t(OTU)

inc_by_season <- lapply(split(rownames(sd), sd$Season), function(samps){
  M <- OTU[, colnames(OTU) %in% samps, drop = FALSE]; M[M > 0] <- 1L
  storage.mode(M) <- "numeric"; M })
set.seed(1)
out_TD <- iNEXT3D(inc_by_season, diversity = "TD", q = c(0,1,2),
                  datatype = "incidence_raw", nboot = 500)
write.csv(as.data.frame(out_TD$TDAsyEst), "H2_iNEXT3D_TD_asymptotic.csv", row.names = FALSE)
ggiNEXT3D(out_TD, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

## ---------- Per-PCR-replicate hillR + frequentist mixed model ----------
# alldat_full[[1]] = one row per PCR replicate; apply the canonical 10,000-read
# floor at the replicate level, then rarefy to the minimum retained depth.
ps_pcr <- prune_samples(sample_sums(alldat_full[[1]]) >= 10000, alldat_full[[1]])
ps_pcr <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(ps_pcr) > 0, ps_pcr)
set.seed(1)
ps_pcr_rar <- rarefy_even_depth(ps_pcr, min(sample_sums(ps_pcr)),
                                replace = FALSE, rngseed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
m  <- as(otu_table(ps_pcr_rar), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps_pcr_rar)) m <- t(m)
md <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps_pcr_rar))
md$Season <- factor(md$Season, levels = c("winter","summer")); md$Year <- factor(md$Year)
md$indivID_glm      <- droplevels(factor(ifelse(is.na(md$indivID) | md$indivID == "",
                                                paste0("unk_", md$sample), md$indivID)))
md$pcr_replicate_id <- droplevels(factor(md$sample))
hill_pcr <- data.frame(q0 = hillR::hill_taxa(m, 0), q1 = hillR::hill_taxa(m, 1),
                       q2 = hillR::hill_taxa(m, 2),
                       Season = md$Season, Year = md$Year,
                       indivID_glm = md$indivID_glm, pcr_replicate_id = md$pcr_replicate_id)

# Fit one model per q; drop random terms if singular, report what converged.
fit_h2_lmm <- function(dat, qcol) {
  ladder <- list(
    "Season + (1|Year) + (1|indivID_glm) + (1|pcr_replicate_id)",
    "Season + (1|Year) + (1|pcr_replicate_id)",
    "Season + (1|pcr_replicate_id)")
  for (rhs in ladder) {
    fit <- tryCatch(lmerTest::lmer(as.formula(paste(qcol, "~", rhs)), data = dat),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(fit) && !lme4::isSingular(fit)) break
  }
  if (is.null(fit) || lme4::isSingular(fit))
    fit <- lm(as.formula(paste(qcol, "~ Season")), data = dat)
  co <- summary(fit)$coefficients
  est <- co["Seasonsummer","Estimate"]; se <- co["Seasonsummer","Std. Error"]
  pv  <- if ("Pr(>|t|)" %in% colnames(co)) co["Seasonsummer","Pr(>|t|)"] else NA
  data.frame(metric = qcol, summer_minus_winter = round(est,3),
             lwr = round(est-1.96*se,3), upr = round(est+1.96*se,3), p = round(pv,4))
}
write.csv(dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("q0","q1","q2"), function(q) fit_h2_lmm(hill_pcr, q))),
          "H2_lmm_season_effect.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---------- Dominance / evenness, top-5 OTUs, coprophilous share ----------
library(phyloseq); library(dplyr)
ps <- alldat$nopool
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (!taxa_are_rows(ps)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)  # taxa x samples
sd  <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps))
rel <- sweep(otu_mat, 2, colSums(otu_mat), "/")

pielou_J <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; (-sum(p*log(p))) / log(length(p)) }
dom <- data.frame(sample = colnames(otu_mat), Season = sd$Season,
                  richness = colSums(otu_mat > 0),
                  top1_prop = apply(rel, 2, max),
                  pielou_J  = apply(rel, 2, pielou_J))
dom %>% group_by(Season) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_richness = round(mean(richness),1),
            mean_top1_prop_pct = round(100*mean(top1_prop),1),
            mean_pielou_J = round(mean(pielou_J),2)) # + Wilcoxon tests -> report_dominance_summary.csv

tax <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"))
seasons <- levels(factor(sd$Season))
top5 <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seasons, function(s){
  shares <- rowMeans(rel[, rownames(sd)[sd$Season == s], drop = FALSE])
  ids <- names(sort(shares, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
  data.frame(Season = s, OTU = ids, mean_pct_share = round(100*shares[ids],2),
             tax[ids, c("Phylum","Class","Order","Family","Genus","Species")]) }))
write.csv(top5, "report_top5_otu_by_season.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Coprophilous-genus screen (COPRO_GENERA list lifted from confirmatory_analysis.R)
COPRO_GENERA <- c("Sordaria","Podospora","Cercophora","Chaetomium","Schizothecium",
                  "Preussia","Sporormiella","Delitschia","Pilobolus","Ascobolus",
                  "Coprinopsis","Saccobolus","Sporormia")
strip_pref <- function(x){ x <- sub("^[a-z]__","",x); x[x=="" | grepl("unidentified",x,TRUE)] <- NA; x }
genus_clean <- strip_pref(tax$Genus)
copro_otus  <- rownames(tax)[!is.na(genus_clean) & genus_clean %in% COPRO_GENERA]
# per-OTU winter/summer mean share + occurrences -> report_coprophilous_by_season(_v2).csv
```

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
#### Documentation notes — Section 5 {.unnumbered}

This dark, winter-associated OTU is an **E1** dark taxon (Section 3.4) — and, being winter-persistent, a candidate to carry into the deferred H3 plant-covariation analysis downstream — and it revises the original "stable cold-adapted *Thelebolus*–*Sporormiella* core" framing: those recognizable coprophilous genera are part of the summer-inflated, activity-tracking tail, not a season-independent core.
:::

## Section 6: Lineage-specific seasonal responses — GLLVM (H1, OTU-resolved) {.page-break-before}

Sections 4 and 5 establish that the community shifts between seasons (H1) and that summer samples gain a long rare tail while becoming more dominance-skewed (H2). This section resolves H1 to the level of individual OTUs. We fit a generalized linear latent-variable model (GLLVM, negative-binomial) of per-OTU counts as a function of Season (winter as reference), with a library-size offset and random intercepts for individual bird and PCR replicate; the model is fitted on the full-complexity, one-row-per-PCR-replicate object (`Scripts/7_gllvm.R`, objects `models/fit_nb_2.rds` and `models/fit_nb_2_2.rds`). It answers which lineages drive the turnover — each with its own model uncertainty — and, through its latent variables, describes the residual co-occurrence that remains after Season is accounted for.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- SEE NOTE: a real scientific limitation, not a status note — you may want one plain sentence of this to survive into the submitted version -->

::: callout-warning
**Fitted on the pre-depth-fix object.** These fits were built on the full-complexity object as it stood *before* the July depth-filter correction: 57 samples (114 PCR-replicate rows) and 327 filtered OTUs, versus the 52-sample / 278-OTU canonical object used everywhere else in this appendix. The library-size offset, per-OTU abundance weights, and the Poisson baseline in Table S-GLLVMa are all reconstructed from that same pre-fix object so the section is internally consistent. The five extra samples and larger OTU set do not change the direction or rank of any result below, but exact coefficients will move slightly when the models are refitted on the corrected object — treat the numbers as robust in sign and rank, provisional in the last digit.
:::
:::

### 6.1 Model choice

```{r tab-gllvm-aic}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_model_comparison.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mc$logLik <- signif(mc$logLik, 4); mc$AIC <- signif(mc$AIC, 5); mc$dAIC <- signif(mc$dAIC, 4)
kable(mc[, c("model", "logLik", "AIC", "dAIC")],
      col.names = c("Model", "logLik", "AIC", "ΔAIC"),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMa. GLLVM model comparison on the same 327-OTU / 114-row response matrix. The negative-binomial fits are dramatically better than the Poisson baseline (strong overdispersion), and two latent variables are preferred over one (ΔAIC ≈ 723). fit_nb_2_2 is the reported model.")
```

The negative-binomial family is strongly favoured over Poisson (the Poisson log-likelihood is worse by \~5 orders of magnitude, the signature of severe count overdispersion), and two latent variables outperform one by ΔAIC ≈ 723. We therefore report `fit_nb_2_2` (negative-binomial, two latent variables).

### 6.2 Which OTUs drive the seasonal turnover

For every OTU we extract the Season coefficient (β on the GLLVM log scale; positive = higher in summer) together with the model's own Wald 95% CI, and flag significance at a Benjamini–Hochberg FDR of 5%.

![](figures/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMa**: Season response of the 30 most abundant OTUs, each with its model 95% CI, coloured by Order; filled points are significant at BH q \< 0.05. Of the 327 modelled OTUs, 209 are significant, and the turnover is strongly asymmetric: 166 OTUs are enriched in summer versus 43 in winter. A further 134 OTUs are near-complete "on/off" seasonal switches (essentially absent in one season); these have real but non-interpretable point estimates (β in the hundreds, or exploding CIs) and are flagged (`separation`) and excluded both from this panel and from Table S-GLLVMb, which reports only well-estimated OTUs; they are retained in the full per-OTU table (`tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv`).

```{r tab-gllvm-otu}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
oc  <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
well <- oc %>% filter(!separation, sig)
fmt <- function(df) df %>% transmute(OTU = taxon, Genus, Order,
                                     beta = round(beta_season, 2),
                                     `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", ci_lo, ci_hi),
                                     `BH q` = signif(p_adj, 2))
kable(well %>% arrange(desc(beta_season)) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>% fmt(),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMb(i). Most strongly summer-enriched well-estimated OTUs (BH q < 0.05).")
kable(well %>% arrange(beta_season) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>% fmt(),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMb(ii). Most strongly winter-enriched well-estimated OTUs (BH q < 0.05). Full per-OTU table: tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv.")
```

Two results connect directly to the dominance analysis (Section 5.4). The coprophilous taxa that dominate summer read share behave differently under the model: OTU636 (*Sporormiella*, β ≈ 17.2) and OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*, β ≈ 17.3) are both significantly summer-enriched, but OTU1 (*Thelebolus*, β ≈ 3.0) is not significant (95% CI crosses zero) — its large summer read share is carried by a few samples and high among-individual variance rather than a model-robust per-OTU shift. On the winter side, the dark taxon OTU1369 (class Dothideomycetes) is significantly winter-enriched (β ≈ −6.9): the GLLVM independently corroborates the dominance/E1 finding that winter's persistent OTU is a taxonomically unresolved lineage.

Aggregating to genus gives the broader pattern:

![](figures/panel_AB_heatmap_barplot_season.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMc**: Genus-level seasonal response. (A) Heatmap of the abundance-weighted mean β per genus; (B) the same as a point-range plot with bootstrapped 95% CIs. Warm = summer-enriched, cool = winter-enriched.

```{r tab-gllvm-genus}

suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
gt <- read.csv("tables/genus_table_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gt %>% transmute(Order, Genus, n_OTUs,
                 `total reads` = round(total_w_abund),
                 `median beta` = round(median_beta_season, 1),

  arrange(desc(`weighted-mean beta`)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table S-GLLVMc. Genus-level seasonal responses (β = summer vs winter, GLLVM log scale) for genera passing the abundance/effect-size thresholds. Full detail in models/genus_table_season.csv.")
```

### 6.3 Residual co-occurrence beyond Season

![](figures/gllvm_residual_ordination.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMb**: Model-based ordination on the two latent variables of `fit_nb_2_2` — the residual OTU co-occurrence structure that remains *after* Season and the random effects are accounted for. Sites are coloured by Season; the eight strongest species loadings are labelled. This is the model-based counterpart to the unconstrained robust-Aitchison PCoA in Section 4.1: because Season is already in the model as a fixed effect, the two seasons overlap substantially here, confirming that Season captures a coherent axis of the community rather than all of its covariation. A small set of winter sites separates along the second latent variable (winter scores are \~3.4× as variable as summer ones on that axis, Fligner–Killeen p = 0.013; seven of the eight most extreme sites are winter). This is specific to that axis and is not a statement about which season is more heterogeneous overall — on the first latent variable summer is the more variable season, and Section 4.2 finds ummer significantly the more dispersed in total composition (mean distance to centroid 24.8 versus 13.6, p = 0.002).

## Section 7: Diet-tracking and Bayesian models — H2 and H3 {.page-break-before}

### 7.1 Diet richness and fungal diversity — Bayesian mechanism (H2)

Section 5 established the coarse prediction of H2: summer communities are richer than winter ones, in step with the richer summer diet. Here we test the finer mechanism directly, on the subset of samples for which we have paired plant ITS2 diet data (**n = 27** dung samples): does an individual sample's fungal diversity track the richness of its own dietary plant community? Fungal Hill diversity is modelled as a function of standardised plant (diet) richness, adjusting for Season, in a Bayesian linear model (brms). H2's mechanism is supported if the plant-richness slope is positive with posterior probability P(slope \> 0) \> 0.95.

The preregistration specified Year and individual bird as random intercepts. At this matched sample size that structure is unidentifiable — 27 of the 27 samples are distinct individuals and Year spans only three levels — and the random-effects model does not converge. We therefore report two complementary, cleanly-converged fixed-effect models that bracket the estimate: a **Season-adjusted** model (`plant_richness + Season + Year`, Year as a fixed effect) and a more parsimonious **drop-Year** model (`plant_richness + Season`). Both use weakly-informative standardised priors (slope \~ Normal(0, 1)).

![](figures/H2_diet_richness_fit.png)

**Figure S9**: Per-sample fungal Hill q1 diversity against rarefied dietary plant richness (n = 27 matched samples), coloured by Season. Both model fits are shown — Season-adjusted (solid) and drop-Year (dashed) — with the 95% credible ribbon for the primary Season-adjusted model. Fitted lines are drawn at the reference Season/Year; the quantity of interest is the common positive slope.

```{r tab-h2mech-compare}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_model_comparison.csv", check.names = FALSE)
mc_disp <- data.frame(
  Model       = mc$model,
  Structure   = mc$formula,
  `Slope (median)` = round(mc$median, 3),
  `95% CrI`   = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", mc$lwr95, mc$upr95),
  `P(slope>0)`= round(mc$P_gt0, 3),
  Divergences = mc$divergences,
  `Clears 0.95?` = ifelse(mc$supported, "yes", "no"),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(mc_disp,
      caption = "Table S12. H2-mechanism: the two complementary Bayesian models of fungal Hill q1 diversity vs. dietary plant richness (standardised slope). Both converge cleanly (0 divergences, Rhat < 1.01) and place the diet-richness slope positive.")
```

Both models place the diet-richness slope firmly positive (medians +0.28 and +0.38 standard deviations of fungal diversity per standard deviation of plant richness), with posterior support of **P(slope \> 0) = 0.92** (Season-adjusted) and **0.96** (drop-Year). The drop-Year model clears the preregistered 0.95 threshold; the Season-adjusted model sits just below it. The direction of the effect is therefore consistent, and the weight of posterior evidence favours the predicted positive diet-richness → fungal-diversity relationship.

![](figures/H2_mechanism_slope_posterior.png)

**Figure S10**: Posterior distribution of the standardised diet-richness slope for both models. The mass of both posteriors lies to the right of zero (dashed line).

The signal is consistent across the choice of Hill order: refitting with richness (q0) and Simpson-equivalent (q2) diversity as the outcome gives positive slopes throughout, with P(slope \> 0) between 0.89 and 0.96 (Table S13). No specification reverses the direction.

```{r tab-h2mech-sens}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
sn <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_sensitivity.csv", check.names = FALSE)
sn_disp <- data.frame(
  `Hill order` = sn$metric,
  Model        = sn$model,
  `Slope (median)` = round(sn$median, 3),
  `95% CrI`    = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", sn$lwr95, sn$upr95),
  `P(slope>0)` = round(sn$P_gt0, 3),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(sn_disp,
      caption = "Table S13. Sensitivity of the diet-richness slope to Hill order (q0 richness, q1 Shannon, q2 Simpson) under both model structures. All twelve estimates are positive.")
```

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Ecological interpretation.** Dietary plant richness is markedly higher in summer than winter, so most of the diet–diversity relationship is expressed through the *seasonal* contrast — which is exactly the diet-driven mechanism H2 proposes: the seasonal diet shift is the dominant axis of variation in propagule supply, and summer's richer plant intake is accompanied by a richer fungal community. Within a single season the diet-richness gradient is short (only a few plant OTUs separate one sample from another), so the per-sample effect is correspondingly modest.

Consistent with a modest, gradient-limited signal at this sample size, the estimate is carried by the samples at the extremes of the diet-richness range: a single leave-one-out omission moves the slope within the ranges in Table S14, and rank (Spearman) correlations within each Season are close to zero — the parametric slope reflects the between-season spread of the gradient more than fine within-season covariation. The honest reading is therefore a **weak, directionally-consistent signal**: fungal diversity does tend to rise with dietary plant richness, primarily at the seasonal scale, but the per-sample effect is not resolved decisively at n = 27 and is a clear target for a larger diet-matched sample.
:::

The honest reading is a directionally-consistent signal: fungal diversity does tend to rise with dietary plant richness, primarily at the seasonal scale, but the per-sample effect is not resolved decisively at n = 27 and is a clear target for a larger diet-matched sample.

```{r tab-h2mech-robust}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
rb <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_robustness.csv", check.names = FALSE)
names(rb) <- c("Check", "Group", "Quantity", "Value")
kable(rb,
      caption = "Table S14. Robustness of the diet-richness slope: leave-one-out influence (frequentist slope, its range across single-sample omissions, and the most influential sample) and within/between-Season Spearman rank correlations.")
```

### 7.2 OTU–plant covariation (H3) - H3 not supported - still working 

Section 7.1 asked whether overall fungal diversity tracks overall diet richness. H3 is finer-grained and taxon-resolved: does each fungal OTU covary with particular diet-plant taxa, and — the preregistered contrast — do recognised coprophilous taxa show the diffuse, non-specific plant associations expected of dung specialists dispersed independently of any host plant, while other taxa may show the tight, single-plant covariation that would flag a likely ingested endophyte passenger? Inference is strictly forward-directional: a tight single-plant association is read as evidence of a likely ingested passenger; a diffuse or absent association is not read as evidence of gut/dung residency.

**Model.** We fit a single hierarchical joint negative-binomial model (brms) to the diet-matched subset. To retain as many matched samples as possible we use the PCR-replicate-level, minimally depth-filtered object (mirroring the GLLVM of Section 6) rather than the collapsed, 10,000-read-filtered object of Sections 4–5; this recovers three additional low-depth winter dung samples that carry paired plant data, raising the matched subset to **n = 30 biological samples (60 PCR-replicate libraries; 19 winter, 11 summer)**. Each fungal OTU count is modelled with a per-replicate log-library-size offset (so shallow libraries are accommodated, not discarded), the six dominant diet-plant genera (rCLR-transformed, standardised) as predictors, Season and Year as population-level covariates, per-OTU varying intercepts and plant slopes (the partial-pooling "joint model"), and a per-OTU biological-sample random effect so the two PCR replicates of a sample are treated as replication rather than independent samples. This substitutes a sample random effect for the preregistered "individual" one (unidentifiable here — nearly every sample is a distinct bird), for the same reason as Section 7.1. Forty-six OTUs present in ≥5 of the 30 samples are modelled. For each OTU we summarise the specificity of its plant coefficients with a Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) of the \|plant slopes\| — ≈1/6 = 0.17 if covariation is spread evenly across all six genera, up to 1 if concentrated on a single plant — and flag a resolved single-plant association when the 90% credible interval of the OTU's strongest plant slope excludes zero. The preregistered contrast compares specificity between FUNGuild-flagged coprophilous OTUs and plant-associated (endophyte/phyllosphere/plant-saprotroph) OTUs. The model converged cleanly (maximum R̂ = 1.004, no divergent transitions).

![](figures/H3_perOTU_plant_coef.png)

**Figure S11**: Posterior-median covariation of each modelled fungal OTU (rows, ordered by specificity and grouped by FUNGuild guild class) with each dominant diet-plant genus (columns), on the log (negative-binomial) scale; red = positive, blue = negative. The three recognised coprophilous taxa (*Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta*, *Sporormiella*) covary *positively* and strongly with *Vaccinium*, whereas most other OTUs covary negatively with it.

```{r tab-h3-spec}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
si <- read.csv("tables/H3_specificity_index.csv", check.names = FALSE)
si_disp <- head(si, 12)
kable(data.frame(
  OTU            = si_disp$OTU_ID,
  Genus          = ifelse(is.na(si_disp$Genus), "—", si_disp$Genus),
  `Prev. (/30)`  = si_disp$prevalence,
  Specificity    = round(si_disp$specificity_HHI, 2),
  `Top plant`    = si_disp$dominant_plant,
  `Top slope [90% CrI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", si_disp$dom_slope_med,
                                  si_disp$dom_slope_lwr90, si_disp$dom_slope_upr90),
  Resolved       = ifelse(si_disp$resolved_single_plant, "yes", "—"),
  Guild          = si_disp$guild_group,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S15. The twelve most plant-specific fungal OTUs (of 46 modelled), ranked by the Herfindahl specificity of their plant coefficients. Only OTU1 (Thelebolus) reaches a resolved single-plant association (its Vaccinium slope's 90% CrI excludes zero). Diffuse baseline (six genera) = 0.17.")
```

**Result.** For almost every OTU the plant covariation is too weak to resolve at this sample size: of the 46 OTUs, **only one — OTU1 (*Thelebolus*) — shows a resolved single-plant association** (a strong positive *Vaccinium* slope, median +2.30 on the log scale, 90% CrI \[0.18, 4.62\]). This single tight association runs *opposite* to the preregistered expectation: *Thelebolus* is a recognised coprophilous dung specialist, not a phyllosphere/endophyte passenger. More generally, the three coprophilous taxa are the *most* plant-concentrated OTUs in the dataset, not the least (Figure S12): the coprophilous group has a higher median specificity than the plant-associated group (0.38 vs 0.30) — the reverse of the predicted "coprophilous = more diffuse" pattern. The contrast is not supported in either direction under uncertainty: a one-sided Wilcoxon test of the preregistered direction gives p = 0.72, and propagating the full posterior, P(coprophilous more diffuse) = 0.36. The genus-list sensitivity grouping (coprophilous = *Thelebolus*/*Sporormiella*/*Coniochaeta*) tells the same story (0.51 vs 0.30).

![](figures/H3_specificity_contrast.png)

**Figure S12**: Per-OTU plant-association specificity (Herfindahl index) by FUNGuild guild class. Contrary to the preregistered prediction, coprophilous OTUs are if anything *more* plant-concentrated than plant-associated ones. Dashed line = maximally-diffuse baseline (1/6).

```{r tab-h3-contrast}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
ct <- read.csv("tables/H3_specificity_contrast.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Grouping                    = ct$grouping,
  `n copro`                   = ct$n_coprophilous,
  `n plant-assoc`             = ct$n_plant_assoc,
  `Copro HHI`                 = round(ct$copro_spec_med, 2),
  `Plant-assoc HHI`           = round(ct$plant_spec_med, 2),
  `Wilcoxon p (copro<plant)`  = round(ct$wilcox_p_copro_lower, 2),
  `P(copro more diffuse)`     = round(ct$P_copro_lower, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S16. Preregistered coprophilous-vs-plant-associated specificity contrast (FUNGuild primary grouping; COPRO_GENERA genus list as sensitivity). Neither grouping supports the predicted 'coprophilous more diffuse' direction. The full per-OTU × plant coefficient table is provided as tables/H3_perOTU_plant_coef.csv (Table S17).")
```

**Interpretation.** H3, as preregistered, is **not supported**: taxonomically recognised coprophilous taxa do *not* show more diffuse plant associations than other taxa — if anything the reverse. The single interpretable plant signal is a *Vaccinium*–*Thelebolus* covariation, and its ecology is the opposite of the "ingested passenger" reading H3 was built to detect: *Thelebolus* is a dung specialist, and *Vaccinium* (with *Empetrum*) is the winter browse of ptarmigan at this site. Because Season is already a covariate this is a within-season-adjusted association, but the residual gradient is short; the most parsimonious reading is that the winter-browse plants and the persistent dung-fungal core co-vary as parallel seasonal signatures of the same samples, not that *Thelebolus* is carried into the gut on *Vaccinium* tissue. This dovetails with Section 6, where *Thelebolus* (OTU1) was the one coprophile *without* a clean seasonal differential-abundance signal, and with the E2 documentation in Section 3.2.

**Limitation.** Even at n = 30 the diet is dominated by a few plant genera (*Betula* near-ubiquitous, then *Vaccinium*/*Empetrum*), so specificity can be assessed over only \~6 genera and the coprophilous group is small (6 OTUs). We therefore report H3 as a directional, exploratory result rather than a decisive test — and, consistent with the forward-directional inference rule, the absence of tight single-plant passenger signatures is **not** evidence that the dung mycobiome is gut-resident. A larger, more diet-even matched sample is the necessary next step.

### 7.3 OTU–plant covariation — GLLVM cross-check (H3)

To check that the H3 verdict of Section 7.2 is not an artefact of one modelling framework, we repeat the analysis with a generalised linear latent-variable model (GLLVM) — the same model-based framework used for the OTU-resolved H1 in Section 6, now with the diet-plant predictors added. Everything about the data is held identical to the Bayesian model: the same PCR-replicate-level matched subset (**n = 30 biological samples, 60 libraries; 46 OTUs present in ≥5 samples**), the same six standardised diet-plant genera (rCLR-transformed), the same per-library log-size offset, and the same specificity index and preregistered coprophilous-vs-plant-associated contrast. Only the estimator differs, which is the point: agreement across two very different fitting machineries is stronger evidence than either alone.

**Model.** Each OTU's counts are modelled with a negative-binomial GLLVM (`gllvm`), with Season and Year as community covariates, a per-OTU (species-specific) *fixed* slope for each plant genus, a biological-sample random row effect (so the two PCR replicates of a sample count as replication, not independent samples), and the log-library-size offset. We fit 0, 1 and 2 residual latent variables and select by AIC; here **num.lv = 0** is preferred — beyond the sample random effect the latent variables capture no further residual co-occurrence (so, unlike Section 6, there is no residual ordination to show). One difference from the Bayesian model is forced by the software: the natural partial-pooling analog (`gllvm`'s `randomX` species-specific *random* slopes) is silently dropped on this dataset, returning no plant-slope parameters at all. We therefore estimate the plant slopes as *fixed* per-OTU coefficients with Wald standard errors — an **unpooled** frequentist estimate that brackets the Bayesian *pooled* one from the other side. Rare on/off OTUs push their fixed coefficients toward ±∞ (near-separation); as in Section 6 these are flagged (16 of 46 OTUs) and excluded from the specificity ranking, contrast and plots, leaving **30 well-estimated OTUs**. Specificity is the same Herfindahl index of the \|plant slopes\|; a *resolved single-plant association* here means the 90 % Wald interval of an OTU's strongest plant slope excludes zero.

```{r tab-h3g-aic}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_model_comparison.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Model    = mc$model,
  `num.lv` = mc$num_lv,
  Plants   = ifelse(mc$plants, "yes", "no"),
  logLik   = round(mc$logLik, 1),
  AIC      = round(mc$AIC, 1),
  dAIC     = round(mc$dAIC, 1),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S18. GLLVM H3 model comparison (AIC). Latent variables add nothing beyond the sample random effect (num.lv = 0 preferred among the plant models), and — notably — the null model with no plant predictors is itself AIC-preferred over the plant models (dAIC ≈ 117): the per-OTU plant slopes do not improve fit enough to justify their parameters, an independent echo of the 'too weak to resolve' result of Section 7.2.")
```

![](figures/gllvm_H3_perOTU_plant_coef.png)

**Figure S13**: Per-OTU fixed plant slopes (GLLVM, log scale; red = positive, blue = negative) for the 30 well-estimated OTUs, rows ordered by specificity and grouped by FUNGuild guild class — the frequentist counterpart of Figure S11. As in the Bayesian model, the coprophilous taxa covary *positively* with *Vaccinium* rather than diffusely.

```{r tab-h3g-spec}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
si <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_specificity_index.csv", check.names = FALSE)
si_disp <- si %>% filter(!separation) %>% head(12)
kable(data.frame(
  OTU            = si_disp$OTU_ID,
  Genus          = ifelse(is.na(si_disp$Genus), "—", si_disp$Genus),
  `Prev. (/30)`  = si_disp$prevalence,
  Specificity    = round(si_disp$specificity_HHI, 2),
  `Top plant`    = si_disp$dominant_plant,
  `Top slope [90% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", si_disp$dom_slope_med,
                                 si_disp$dom_slope_lwr90, si_disp$dom_slope_upr90),
  Resolved       = ifelse(si_disp$resolved_single_plant, "yes", "—"),
  Guild          = si_disp$guild_group,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S19. The twelve most plant-specific well-estimated OTUs under the GLLVM, ranked by Herfindahl specificity. Without the Bayesian model's shrinkage the unpooled Wald intervals resolve many more single-plant slopes; the strongest resolved coprophilous signal is Sporormiella (OTU636) with Vaccinium. Diffuse baseline (six genera) = 0.17.")
```

**Result.** The GLLVM reaches the **same verdict as the Bayesian model — H3 is not supported** — and does so through instructively different intermediate numbers. Because the fixed-slope estimator applies no shrinkage, its Wald intervals resolve **15 of the 30** well-estimated OTUs to a single-plant association (versus 1 of 46 under the pooled Bayesian model). But those resolved associations are spread across guilds rather than concentrated in the non-coprophilous taxa H3 predicts, so they do *not* produce the specificity difference the hypothesis requires. On the preregistered contrast the coprophilous group is **not** resolvably more diffuse than the plant-associated group: median specificity 0.21 (coprophilous) vs 0.24 (plant-associated), one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.42, and propagating the Wald uncertainty P(coprophilous more diffuse) = 0.64 — straddling the no-difference value of 0.5. The genus-list sensitivity grouping runs the other way (0.25 vs 0.24, p = 0.81). And, as above, AIC prefers the plant-free null model outright. The strongest resolved coprophilous signal is again a *positive Vaccinium* slope — here *Sporormiella* (OTU636, +12.3, 90 % CI \[6.7, 17.8\]), the *Sporormiella* counterpart of the Bayesian model's *Vaccinium*–*Thelebolus* signal — the opposite of the diffuse, passenger-free pattern H3 expects of a dung specialist.

![](figures/gllvm_H3_specificity_contrast.png)

**Figure S14**: Per-OTU GLLVM specificity by FUNGuild guild class (frequentist counterpart of Figure S12). Coprophilous OTUs are not resolvably more diffuse than plant-associated ones. Dashed line = maximally-diffuse baseline (1/6).

```{r tab-h3g-contrast}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
ct <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_specificity_contrast.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Grouping                    = ct$grouping,
  `n copro`                   = ct$n_coprophilous,
  `n plant-assoc`             = ct$n_plant_assoc,
  `Copro HHI`                 = round(ct$copro_spec_med, 2),
  `Plant-assoc HHI`           = round(ct$plant_spec_med, 2),
  `Wilcoxon p (copro<plant)`  = round(ct$wilcox_p_copro_lower, 2),
  `P(copro more diffuse)`     = round(ct$P_copro_lower, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S20. GLLVM coprophilous-vs-plant-associated specificity contrast (FUNGuild primary; COPRO_GENERA genus list as sensitivity), the frequentist counterpart of Table S16. Neither grouping supports the predicted 'coprophilous more diffuse' direction. The full per-OTU × plant coefficient table (with Wald z, p and BH-q) is provided as tables/gllvm_H3_perOTU_plant_coef.csv.")
```

**Interpretation.** Two independent frameworks — a partial-pooling Bayesian joint model and an unpooled frequentist GLLVM — give the same answer: recognised coprophilous taxa are **not** more diffuse in their plant associations than other taxa, so H3 as preregistered is not supported, and the one robust piece of ecology (a positive coprophile–*Vaccinium* covariation, *Thelebolus* under one model, *Sporormiella* under the other) is the reverse of the ingested-passenger signature the test was built to detect. The two models disagree only on how many single-plant slopes count as "resolved," and that gap is exactly the expected footprint of shrinkage — the pooled model is conservative, the unpooled one liberal — not an ecological disagreement. Consistent with the forward-directional inference rule, neither the sparse Bayesian resolutions nor the plentiful GLLVM ones are read as evidence about gut residency; the honest reading remains that these winter-browse plants and the persistent dung-fungal core co-vary as parallel seasonal signatures, and that a larger, more diet-even matched sample is needed to test single-taxon passenger transport directly.
