## Section 8: Functional guilds — FUNGuild {.page-break-before}

Sections 3–6 characterise the seasonal shift *taxonomically* — which lineages turn over between winter and summer. This section asks what that community **does**: each OTU is assigned to a functional guild, and the guild composition of the dung mycobiome is compared across seasons. It is the descriptive counterpart to Section 9, which puts the same trait → season link inside a joint species distribution model. The two are deliberately built on the **same classification rule** so their results are directly comparable, but they differ in scope: Section 8 works on read shares across **all 1129 OTUs** of the canonical 52-sample object (no prevalence filter, because this is a description of where the reads go), whereas Section 9 models the 226 OTUs that pass its prevalence threshold. All results here are produced by `Scripts/8_functional_guilds.R`.

### 8.1 Guild assignment and the classification rule

Guild annotation uses **FUNGuild** (Nguyen et al. 2016), run through its command-line tool against each OTU's own taxonomy string, so that assignments are made at the finest rank available per OTU (species, genus, family or order) rather than by a single-rank lookup. **693 of the 1129 canonical OTUs (61.4%) receive a guild call** at a usable confidence ranking; the remaining 436 return no assignment — either because no matching taxonomy record exists in the FUNGuild database or because the match carries no ranked guild.

FUNGuild returns compound guild strings rather than a single label — for example `|Dung Saprotroph|-Endophyte-Plant Saprotroph-Undefined Saprotroph`. OTUs are collapsed to a single class by a priority rule (first match wins): dung saprotroph → plant-associated → pathotroph, with anything else falling to *other assigned* or *unassigned* (no FUNGuild call at all). Coprophily takes precedence deliberately: it is the guild the study is about, and it would otherwise be absorbed into a generic saprotroph category. An OTU counts as a dung saprotroph if FUNGuild lists `Dung Saprotroph` **or** its genus is one of the recognised coprophilous genera used throughout this appendix (Section 3.2). This is the identical rule used for the Section-10 guild trait.

```{r tab-guild-crosswalk}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cw <- read.csv("tables/guild_scheme_crosswalk.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lv <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
        "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
cw <- cw[order(match(cw$guild_display, lv)), ]
kable(data.frame(
  `Guild (Section 8)`      = cw$guild_display,
  `Class (Section 9)`     = cw$guild_class,
  `n OTUs`                 = cw$n_OTUs,
  Note                     = cw$note,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-GUILDa. Crosswalk between the Section 8 display guilds and the Section 9 model trait, with OTU counts (1129 canonical OTUs). The two schemes are the same priority rule; they differ only in that Section 9's `other` class is split here according to whether the OTU carries a FUNGuild annotation at all.")
```

### 8.2 Guild composition shifts sharply between seasons

![](figures/Fig1_guild_season.png)

**Figure S-GUILDa**: Functional-guild composition of the dung mycobiome. **(A)** Per-sample guild read share, one stacked bar per dung sample, faceted by season and ordered within each season by dung-saprotroph share. **(B)** Per-sample read share by guild and season; boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, and marks give the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum result (\* q \< 0.05, \*\* q \< 0.01, ns = not significant). **(C)** Mean guild read share by season and year, showing that the shift recurs in all three years. Colours are the Okabe–Ito colourblind-safe palette throughout.

Panels **(A)** and **(B)** here are the same object, rule and test as main-text **Fig. 1B–C** (Section 10.1) — the same result, not a second analysis. This figure is retained because panel **(C)**, the Season × Year consistency check of Section 8.3, has no main-text counterpart.

The seasonal contrast is large and concerns primarily two of the five guilds. **Dung saprotrophs rise from 13.6% of winter reads to 51.5% in summer**, while the **unassigned/dark fraction falls from 51.1% to 21.0%** — that is, roughly half of a typical winter sample consists of reads that FUNGuild cannot place at all, whereas a typical summer sample is dominated by recognised coprophilous fungi. Equivalently, the proportion of reads landing on a guild-annotated OTU rises from **49% in winter to 79% in summer**.

```{r tab-guild-season}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
g <- read.csv("tables/guild_season_readshare.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
kable(data.frame(
  Guild            = g$Guild,
  `Summer mean %`  = pc(g$mean_summer),
  `Winter mean %`  = pc(g$mean_winter),
  `Summer median %`= pc(g$median_summer),
  `Winter median %`= pc(g$median_winter),
  `Detected (S/W)` = paste0(g$prevalence_summer, "/", g$prevalence_winter),
  `p`              = signif(g$p_value, 2),
  `q (BH)`         = ifelse(is.na(g$q_value), "—", signif(g$q_value, 2)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-GUILDb. Per-sample guild read shares by season (26 samples per season), with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment across the five guilds. 'Detected' gives the number of samples in which the guild occurs at all. The final row is a robustness check, not part of the BH family: it restricts the dung-saprotroph guild to OTUs matching a recognised coprophilous genus, discarding those assigned on the FUNGuild string alone.")
```

**The dung-saprotroph result does not depend on how generously that guild is defined.** The rule counts an OTU as coprophilous if FUNGuild lists `Dung Saprotroph` *or* its genus is a recognised coprophilous genus. Restricting it to the genus criterion alone drops 24 of the 37 OTUs and still gives **45.7% summer versus 8.5% winter** (p = 0.00094; final row of Table S-GUILDb). The signal is concentrated in a few abundant taxa — OTU1 (*Thelebolus*), OTU636 (*Sporormiella*) and OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*) are the three largest contributors — which is consistent with the dominance analysis of Section 5.4 and with the differential-abundance results of Section 6, where *Sporormiella* OTU636 and *Coniochaeta* OTU1225 are both significantly summer-elevated.

### 8.3 The guild shift recurs in all three years

```{r tab-guild-year}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
sy <- read.csv("tables/guild_season_year_readshare.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lv <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
        "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
cells <- c("Winter 2022","Winter 2023","Winter 2024","Summer 2022","Summer 2023","Summer 2024")
sy$cell <- factor(paste(sy$Season, sy$Year), levels = cells)
mat <- tapply(sy$mean_share, list(factor(sy$Guild, levels = lv), sy$cell),
              function(z) z[1])
kable(cbind(Guild = lv, as.data.frame(round(100 * mat, 1), check.names = FALSE)),
      row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-GUILDc. Mean per-sample guild read share (%) by season and year. Cell sizes: winter 10/9/7 and summer 9/9/8 samples for 2022/2023/2024.")
```

Panel C of Figure S-GUILDa and Table S-GUILDc show the same ordering in every year: **the dung-saprotroph share is higher in summer than in winter in 2022, 2023 and 2024** (41.3% vs 24.5%, 68.3% vs 10.9%, and 44.0% vs 1.7% respectively). Within-year tests are significant for 2023 (q = 0.027) and marginal for 2024 (q = 0.053) but not for 2022 (q = 0.74), where two unusually coprophile-rich winter samples raise the winter mean and its variance. The direction is therefore consistent across all three years while the magnitude varies. This is the functional-guild analogue of the H1 result in Section 4.2, and the two agree closely: the compositional Season × Year interaction is significant there (p = 0.011), and the per-year breakdown ranks the years in the same order as the guild data — 2023 strongest, 2024 intermediate, 2022 weakest (Table S5b). Given three years and modest per-cell sample sizes, the safe reading is that the seasonal shift is directionally reproducible but of year-varying magnitude, not that it has a constant effect size.

::: {.callout-note when-profile="docs"}
**Interpretation and caveats.**

**What this adds.** The guild layer reproduces the seasonal signal independently of taxonomy and gives it a functional reading: summer dung supports an actively coprophilous community, winter dung does not. Section 9 tests the same link within a joint model and reaches a concordant conclusion — guild predicts seasonal *occurrence*, with dung saprotrophs more likely to occur in summer (posterior support 0.96) — so the descriptive and model-based views agree.

**Relation to the dark taxa (E1).** The winter unassigned share here (51.1%) closely tracks the dark-taxa share reported in Section 3.4 (51.3% of winter reads), but the two are **not the same set**: "unassigned" here means no FUNGuild annotation (436 OTUs), while "dark" in Section 3.4 means no confident genus in the canonical taxonomy (493 OTUs). They share 390 OTUs, and 103 OTUs lack a genus yet still receive a FUNGuild call at family or order level. The definitions coincide in winter but diverge in summer (21.0% unassigned versus 31.2% dark), so the two figures should not be used interchangeably. Section 3.4 establishes that a substantial part of this winter fraction is genuinely novel rather than merely absent from reference databases; the functional consequence is that **winter guild composition is the least well characterised part of this dataset**, and its apparent depletion of coprophiles is partly a statement about annotation coverage.

**Limitations.** (i) Read share is not biomass: PCR and copy-number biases mean these proportions describe sequence abundance, not fungal abundance. (ii) FUNGuild assignments are database-derived and inherit its taxonomic and geographic biases; assignments made at family or order level are necessarily coarser than species-level ones, and confidence rankings (Table S-GUILDb does not stratify by them) are `Probable` for the majority of assigned OTUs. (iii) The compositional constraint discussed above means that a guild's decline in relative terms need not imply any absolute decline. (iv) A guild label describes an ecological capability inferred from relatives, not a verified activity in this substrate.

**Supersedes.** The preliminary guild percentages previously recorded in this section were an interim workspace check that predated the finalized script; they were not reproducible from any committed code. The values above are produced by `Scripts/8_functional_guilds.R` and are reproducible from the staged CSVs in `tables/`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Section 9's residual `other` class mixes OTUs that *do* carry a FUNGuild call with 46 that have a taxonomic genus but **no** guild annotation at all; the latter carry roughly a tenth of winter reads. That conflation is harmless for a model trait but misleading in a read-share figure, so the two are separated here into **Other assigned** and folded into **Unassigned / dark** respectively. Table S-GUILDa reconciles the two schemes.

**Why FUNGuild and not FungalTraits.** Both annotation sources were built and compared. `fungaltraits_otu` (genus-level lookup via the `fungaltraits` package) covers 195 of 1129 OTUs (17%) and is a **strict subset** of the FUNGuild annotation (700 OTUs, 62%) — it contributes no unique coverage. On the 195 OTUs both annotate they agree on the exact `Guild` string only 37% of the time (49% on trophic mode), because collapsing to one record per genus discards the species-level resolution FUNGuild's per-OTU run retains. FUNGuild is therefore used as the sole guild source; FungalTraits is retained only as a coarse sensitivity check, and guild calls are never merged between the two for the same OTU.

**Means and medians tell different parts of this story, and both are reported.** For the plant-associated and pathotroph guilds the seasonal *means* are nearly identical (18.0% vs 23.4%, and 4.7% vs 5.8%) while the *medians* differ several-fold (2.1% vs 18.4%, and 0.1% vs 3.8%). The rank-based tests follow the medians and are significant for both. The reason is compositional rather than ecological: because dung saprotrophs occupy so much of a typical summer sample, every other guild is compressed toward zero in most summer samples, while a small number of summer samples in which coprophiles are absent carry large plant-associated or pathotroph fractions and pull the summer means back up. These guilds are better described as **relatively displaced in summer** than as absolute winter specialists — a limitation inherent to read shares, which are constrained to sum to one.
:::

## Section 9: Joint species distribution model — HMSC (H1 synthesis) {.page-break-before}

Sections 4–6 treat the seasonal signal one lens at a time: community dissimilarity (H1), per-sample diversity (H2), and per-OTU differential abundance (GLLVM). This section brings them into a single hierarchical model. We fit a joint species distribution model (HMSC — Hierarchical Modelling of Species Communities; `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`) that simultaneously (i) partitions each OTU's variance among Season, Year, and the nested sampling structure; (ii) asks whether an OTU's functional guild predicts how it responds to Season (the trait → environment link); (iii) recovers each OTU's seasonal niche for a like-for-like cross-check against the Section-6 GLLVM; (iv) estimates the residual co-occurrence left once Season, Year and traits are accounted for; and (v) tests for phylogenetic signal in seasonal niches. It is the model-based synthesis of the H1 story, fitted directly on the corrected canonical data (unlike the Section-6 GLLVM, which predates the depth-filter fix).

### 9.1 Model, design, and what is (and isn't) trustworthy

The model is fitted on the one-row-per-PCR-replicate object (`alldat_full$nopool`; 109 replicate rows from 55 biological dung samples), retaining the **226 OTUs present in ≥ 5 replicates** — the same prevalence rule used for the GLLVM/H3 analyses. Two response formulations are fitted in parallel: a **CLR-transformed abundance** model (Gaussian; CLR is the compositional normalisation in place of a library-size offset) and a **presence/absence** model (probit). Fixed effects are **Season** (winter as reference) **+ Year**; the species trait is the five-level functional **guild** class derived from FUNGuild (dung saprotroph, plant-associated, pathotroph, dark/unassigned, other — assigned by the priority rule in `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`, counts below). Random effects are latent factors at two levels: **biological sample** (the dung dropping, grouping its two PCR replicates) and **PCR replicate**.

```{r tab-hmsc-guild}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
og <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_otu_guild.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gt <- as.data.frame(table(factor(og$guild_class,
        levels = c("dung_saprotroph","plant_associated","pathotroph","dark_unassigned","other"))))
kable(data.frame(`Guild group` = gt$Var1, `n OTUs` = gt$Freq, check.names = FALSE),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCa. Functional-guild composition of the 226 modelled OTUs. FUNGuild returns a compound guild string per OTU; these are resolved to one class by the hierarchical priority rule in `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`, shared verbatim with Section 8. Dark/unassigned and 'other' together dominate the count — the modest coprophilous set (14 OTUs) nonetheless carries the strongest seasonal signal (Section 9.3–10.4).")
```

An **individual-bird** random level was deliberately **not** included. Microsatellite genotyping succeeded for only a handful of repeat birds, so a bird level (with unidentified droppings entered as singletons) would have \~51 units against 55 biological samples — effectively one-to-one with the sample level, confounding the two sets of latent factors. In the three-level version this stopped the CLR community-level parameters from converging and made the variance partition unstable; dropping it (leaving sample + PCR, mirroring the GLLVM's `(1 | Sample_ID_field)`) resolved both. Each model was fitted with four chains (1000 samples, thinning 50, 25,000 transient iterations).

```{r tab-hmsc-conv}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cv <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_convergence_psrf.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lab <- c(clr = "CLR (abundance)", pa = "Probit (occurrence)", clr_phylo = "CLR + phylogeny")
kable(data.frame(
  Model = lab[cv$model],
  `Beta PSRF (median)` = cv$beta_psrf_med,
  `Beta % < 1.1` = cv$beta_pct_below_1.1,
  `Gamma PSRF (median)` = cv$gamma_psrf_med,
  `Gamma PSRF (max)` = cv$gamma_psrf_max,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCb. Gelman–Rubin convergence (potential scale reduction factor, PSRF) for the per-OTU niches (Beta) and the trait → response link (Gamma). The probit and phylogenetic models converge well; the CLR-Gaussian community-level Gamma does not (median 1.46). We therefore read the guild → Season inference (Section 9.3) from the probit model, and use the CLR model only for the variance partition and per-OTU niches, where it is well behaved.")
```

::: callout-note
**How to read the two response models.** Convergence is honest and not uniform. The **probit (occurrence)** model converges cleanly throughout (Beta median PSRF ≈ 1.01, 99.6% of Beta parameters below 1.1; Gamma median ≈ 1.01) and is the model we trust for the **guild → Season** statement. The **CLR (abundance)** model's per-OTU niches (Beta) and variance partition are well behaved and used as such, but its community-level **Gamma did not converge** (median PSRF ≈ 1.46) — so we do *not* quote CLR guild-response coefficients. This is the expected behaviour of a Gaussian JSDM with latent factors on a small, sparse compositional dataset, and it is why the two formulations are reported side by side rather than one alone.
:::

### 9.2 Variance partitioning: a reproducible seasonal axis within large individual heterogeneity

For every OTU the model decomposes the explained variance in CLR abundance into contributions from Season, Year, and the two random levels. Averaged across OTUs, **Season and Year together account for \~20% of per-OTU variance** (Season \~11%, Year \~8%), with the remainder carried by among-sample (biological dropping) and among-replicate structure.

![](figures/hmsc_variance_partition.png)

**Figure S-HMSCa**: Per-OTU variance partitioning (CLR abundance). Each vertical bar is one OTU; colours give the proportion of that OTU's variance attributable to Season, Year, the biological-sample random level, and the PCR-replicate random level. The Season + Year share is modest but pervasive across the community; individual-dropping heterogeneity (sample level) is the single largest component.

```{r tab-hmsc-vp}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
vp <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_variance_partition.csv", check.names = FALSE)
comp <- c("Season","Year","Random: sample","Random: pcr")
cw  <- colMeans(vp[, comp])
byg <- aggregate(vp[, comp], list(Guild = vp$guild), mean)
tabb <- rbind(data.frame(Guild = "all OTUs (community mean)", t(cw), check.names = FALSE), byg)
tabb[, comp] <- round(tabb[, comp] * 100, 1)
kable(tabb, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Guild group", "Season %", "Year %", "Sample %", "PCR %"),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCc. Mean percentage of per-OTU variance attributed to each component, community-wide and by guild. The Season share is consistent across guilds and, at the community level (~11%), closely matches the Season effect size from the PERMANOVA in Section 4.2 (R² = 0.11) — two very different models converging on the same magnitude of seasonal turnover.")
```

The ecological reading is deliberately two-sided but coherent. The **seasonal axis is real and reproducible** — its community-mean magnitude (\~11%) independently recovers the PERMANOVA R² of 0.11 from Section 4.2 — yet at the level of an individual OTU it is *modest relative to how much dung communities differ from one dropping to the next*. In other words, HMSC formalises what the ordination and dominance analyses already suggested: season shifts the community in a consistent direction, on top of large individual-level variability. This decomposition, broken down by guild exactly as in Table S-HMSCc, is Figure 5B of the main text (Section 10.5).

### 9.3 Guild predicts seasonal occurrence — the coprophilous summer signature, formalised

The trait → environment matrix (Gamma) asks whether an OTU's guild predicts its seasonal response. Read from the well-converged probit model, it does. Relative to the winter reference, **dung saprotrophs are markedly more likely to occur in summer** (the reference-guild Season effect is positive with posterior support 0.96), and the yeast-rich "other" group shows the same direction (support 0.83); **pathotrophs lean the opposite way**, toward winter (support 0.85 in the negative direction). Plant-associated and dark/unassigned taxa show no clear guild-level seasonal preference.

![](figures/hmsc_probit_gamma.png)

**Figure S-HMSCb**: Trait → environment link (Gamma) from the probit occurrence model. Cells show the posterior support for each guild's response to Season and Year; the dung-saprotroph summer signal and the guild-structured Year (2024) shift are the supported effects. Red = positive (summer / higher), blue = negative.

```{r tab-hmsc-gamma}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
g <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_probit_gamma_CrI.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
g <- g[g$covariate == "Seasonsummer", ]
g$trait <- sub("^guild", "", g$trait)
g$trait[g$trait == "(Intercept)"] <- "dung saprotroph (reference)"
kable(data.frame(
  `Guild (trait)` = g$trait,
  `Gamma (summer)` = round(g$mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", g$CrI_2.5, g$CrI_97.5),
  `Support P(>0)` = round(g$support, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCd. Probit Gamma — guild trait → probability of summer occurrence. The reference row is the dung-saprotroph guild's own Season effect; the other rows are deviations from it. Support is the posterior probability that the coefficient exceeds zero (values near 1 = summer, near 0 = winter).")
```

This is the guild-level counterpart to the taxonomic and dominance results (Sections 3.2, 5.4): the recognised coprophilous fungi — *Sporormiella*, *Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta* — are not a fixed cold-adapted core but a **summer-occurring dung guild**, consistent with the richer, more fungal-propagule-laden summer diet. HMSC states that pattern as a trait effect estimated across all 226 OTUs at once, rather than genus by genus.

### 9.4 Per-OTU seasonal niches, and agreement with the GLLVM

Extracting each OTU's Season coefficient (Beta) from the CLR model recovers the same lineages at the individual level. The **most strongly summer-shifted OTUs are exactly the coprophilous dung saprotrophs** — *Sporormiella* (OTU636), *Thelebolus* (OTU1) and *Coniochaeta* (OTU1225) — while the **most strongly winter-shifted OTUs are dark/unassigned taxa**, led by OTU1369, the same taxonomically unresolved Dothideomycete that anchors winter dominance in Sections 5.4 and the E1 dark-taxa analysis (Section 3.4).

![](figures/hmsc_beta_season.png)

**Figure S-HMSCc**: Per-OTU seasonal niche (HMSC CLR Beta on Season; positive = summer), for the 25 most summer- and 25 most winter-shifted OTUs, coloured by guild, with 95% credible intervals. The summer extreme is dominated by dung saprotrophs (warm) and yeasts; the winter extreme by dark/unassigned taxa.

```{r tab-hmsc-beta}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
b <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_beta_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fmt <- function(d) d %>% transmute(
  OTU = OTU_ID, Genus = ifelse(is.na(Genus), "—", Genus), Guild = guild,
  Beta = round(beta_season_mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", beta_season_CrI2.5, beta_season_CrI97.5),
  Support = round(beta_season_support, 2))
kable(b %>% arrange(desc(beta_season_mean)) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmt(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(i). Most strongly summer-shifted OTUs (HMSC CLR Beta on Season).")
kable(b %>% arrange(beta_season_mean) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmt(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(ii). Most strongly winter-shifted OTUs. Wide credible intervals on the summer coprophiles reflect the abundance model's larger uncertainty; direction and support are nonetheless consistent. Full table: tables/hmsc_beta_season.csv.")
```

The same per-OTU niche estimated on the **occurrence** scale — the probit model, whose Beta parameters are the ones that converge cleanly (Table S-HMSCb) — is considerably sharper: 55 of the 226 OTUs have a Season coefficient whose 95% credible interval excludes zero, against 4 in the abundance model. The two formulations rank the community's seasonal responses consistently (Spearman ρ = 0.82), and their per-OTU estimates aggregate to the guild-level Gamma of Section 9.3 to within 0.04, so nothing here contradicts the results above. What the occurrence scale does change is *which* taxa sit at the summer extreme. In abundance the coprophiles lead outright; in occurrence the shift is community-wide (157 of 226 OTUs point towards summer, median +0.70) and the extreme is occupied by cold-adapted basidiomycete yeasts — *Vishniacozyma*, *Mrakia*, *Piskurozyma*, *Phenoliferia* — with *Sporormiella* (OTU636) the only dung saprotroph in the top 25 and the mean dung-saprotroph rank falling to 125 of 226 (from 54 in abundance). The distinction is ecologically substantive rather than a modelling artefact: coprophilous fungi are what summer dung is largely *made of* in read share, but they are not the taxa that most reliably *appear* in summer. The winter extreme is unchanged and, if anything, more strongly resolved — dark/unassigned taxa and pathotrophs, with OTU1369 the most winter-shifted OTU in the community (β = −2.25, 95% CrI \[−3.53, −1.08\]). Both scales are carried forward: Figure 5A in Section 10.5 plots this occurrence-scale niche, while the abundance-scale table above remains the one comparable with the GLLVM below.

```{r tab-hmsc-beta-probit}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
bp <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_probit_beta_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fmtp <- function(d) d %>% transmute(
  OTU = OTU_ID, Genus = ifelse(is.na(Genus), "—", Genus), Guild = guild,
  Beta = round(beta_season_mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", beta_season_CrI2.5, beta_season_CrI97.5),
  Support = round(beta_season_support, 3))
kable(bp %>% arrange(desc(beta_season_mean)) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmtp(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(iii). Most strongly summer- and winter-shifted OTUs on the occurrence scale (HMSC probit Beta on Season; positive = more likely to occur in summer). Unlike the abundance model, these intervals are mostly resolved — 55 of 226 OTUs exclude zero. Full table: tables/hmsc_probit_beta_season.csv.")
kable(bp %>% arrange(beta_season_mean) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmtp(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(iv). Most strongly winter-shifted OTUs, occurrence scale. Support is the posterior probability that the coefficient exceeds zero.")
```

Because the GLLVM (Section 6) is an independent model — negative-binomial counts rather than CLR abundance, a different random-effect structure, and fitted on a different OTU snapshot — the two provide a genuine cross-method check. Their per-OTU Season coefficients agree well.

![](figures/hmsc_vs_gllvm_season.png)

**Figure S-HMSCd**: HMSC (CLR Beta) versus GLLVM Season coefficient, one point per shared OTU (n = 139 after excluding the GLLVM's on/off near-separation OTUs, whose ±10³ coefficients are not comparable), coloured by guild. The two independent joint models rank the OTUs' seasonal responses consistently (**Spearman ρ = 0.70**), a strong convergent-validity result for H1 at OTU resolution.

### 9.5 Residual co-occurrence beyond Season

The biological-sample latent factors capture the co-occurrence structure that remains once Season, Year and guild are accounted for — pairs of OTUs that rise and fall together across droppings for reasons the fixed effects do not explain.

![](figures/hmsc_omega_sample.png)

**Figure S-HMSCe**: Residual OTU–OTU association matrix (biological-sample level), showing only associations supported at ≥ 0.95 posterior probability and restricted to OTUs with at least one such association, ordered by hierarchical clustering. Red = positive residual co-occurrence, blue = negative. Blocks of positively associated OTUs indicate sub-communities that track together beyond the seasonal signal — candidate co-dispersed or co-sourced groups for follow-up.

### 9.6 Phylogenetic signal in seasonal niches

Adding the OTU phylogeny to the CLR model estimates rho, the degree to which closely related fungi share environmental niches. The signal is substantial and well-identified.

```{r tab-hmsc-rho}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
rh <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_rho_phylo.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  `ρ (median)` = round(rh$median, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", rh$CrI_2.5, rh$CrI_97.5),
  `P(ρ>0)` = rh$P_gt0, ESS = rh$ess, PSRF = round(rh$psrf, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCf. Phylogenetic signal parameter ρ from the phylogeny-augmented CLR model. Adding the phylogeny leaves the per-OTU niches and trait link essentially unchanged (Beta / Gamma correlation with the main model ≈ 0.94 / 0.90), so ρ is a genuine additional signal rather than a re-description of the fixed effects.")
```

With **ρ ≈ 0.72 (95% CrI \[0.60, 0.80\], P(ρ \> 0) = 1)**, seasonal niches are **phylogenetically conserved**: related lineages tend to shift together between winter and summer. This dovetails with the guild result — because guild is itself partly phylogenetically structured, the coprophilous summer signature is echoed as a broader phylogenetic pattern. It is reported as a secondary, exploratory result (the phylogeny-augmented model is a supplementary variant), but it is a clean, non-trivial one.

### 9.7 What the model predicts — and its honest limit

Finally, HMSC quantifies how much of the community it actually explains, in-sample versus out-of-sample (two-fold cross-validation, with folds split by biological sample so PCR replicates never leak across folds).

![](figures/hmsc_R2_explanatory_vs_cv.png)

**Figure S-HMSCf**: Explanatory (in-sample) versus two-fold cross-validated per-OTU R² for the CLR model. Points lie far below the 1:1 line: the model fits the observed communities well but does not predict held-out droppings.

```{r tab-hmsc-r2}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
r2 <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_predictive_R2_summary.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lab <- c(clr = "CLR (abundance)", pa = "Probit (occurrence)")
kable(data.frame(
  Model = lab[r2$model],
  `Explanatory R²` = round(r2$mean_expl_R2, 3),
  `2-fold CV R²` = ifelse(is.na(r2$mean_cv_R2), "—", round(r2$mean_cv_R2, 3)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCg. Community-mean explanatory vs cross-validated fit. Explanatory R² is moderate; cross-validated R² is near zero.")
```

The explanatory fit is moderate (community-mean R² ≈ 0.46 for the abundance model) but **cross-validated R² is near zero** — the model does not predict the fungal community of a dropping it has not seen. Far from undercutting the story, this is the quantitative statement of it: the seasonal and guild effects documented above are **real and directional but small against the dominant, idiosyncratic variation among individual droppings**. A ptarmigan's dung mycobiome is shaped by season in a reproducible way, yet remains largely individual — which is exactly what a transient, diet- and propagule-sourced community should look like, and a useful caution for anyone hoping to read season directly off a single sample.

**In summary**, HMSC does not overturn any earlier result; it unifies them and adds two things the single-lens analyses could not: a variance decomposition that sizes the seasonal signal against individual heterogeneity (and independently recovers the PERMANOVA effect size), and a formal trait- and phylogeny-level account of *why* the seasonal turnover looks the way it does — a summer-occurring coprophilous dung guild, phylogenetically conserved, riding on top of large among-individual variability.

## Section 10: Main-test figures {.page-break-before}

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Sections 2–9 document the analyses in full. This section collects the figures that appear in the **main manuscript**, which present a deliberately reduced selection of those results for a general readership. It exists so that every main-text figure has exactly one authoritative definition.

**How this section works.**

-   Each main figure appears **once**, embedded from `figures/main/`, with its **full build code in the collapsible drop-down** beneath it (HTML version).
-   Every figure is written in three formats to the same stem: **`.png` and `.jpg` at 600 dpi** (raster, for whichever a submission system demands) and **`.pdf`** (vector, for print). The appendix embeds the PNG.
-   That code chunk **is the source of truth** for the figure. There is no parallel copy in `Scripts/`; nothing else generates these files.
-   The chunks are `eval: false`, so rendering this appendix never rebuilds a figure. To rebuild one after editing its chunk, run the runner from the `Supplementary/` directory:

``` bash
conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig1-build
```

-   Each figure carries a one-line **provenance cross-reference** naming the thematic sections its inputs come from.
-   The thematic sections keep their own supplementary version of a plot only where it is genuinely different (a different object, more ranks, unfiltered); where it would be the same object, they cross-reference here instead.

**File-naming rule.** Supplementary figure files begin with `S`; main-text figure files are `Fig<N>_<slug>` and live in `figures/main/`. (One legacy exception is pending: `figures/Fig1_guild_season.png` is the *supplementary* Figure S-GUILDa of Section 8 and is scheduled for renaming.)
:::

### 10.1 Figure 1 — Composition and function of the dung mycobiome

*Provenance: Fig. 1A uses the genus-level composition of Section 3.1; Fig. 1B–C the guild assignments of Section 8.2. All three panels are computed on the canonical 52-sample object (`alldat$nopool`), and A and B share one sample axis.*

![](figures/main/Fig1_composition_function.png)

**Figure 1**: Composition and function of the willow ptarmigan dung mycobiome across seasons. **(A)** Per-sample genus-level read share — the nine most abundant genera, all remaining named genera pooled as *Other genera*, and reads on OTUs with no confident genus assignment as *Unassigned*. **(B)** Per-sample functional-guild read share for the **same 52 samples in the same order**, so each column is the same dropping in both panels; samples are ordered within each season by descending dung-saprotroph share. **(C)** Per-sample guild read share by season; boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, and marks give the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum result across the five guilds (\* q \< 0.05, \*\* q \< 0.01, ns = not significant). *Thelebolus* in (A) and the dung-saprotroph guild in (B) intentionally share one colour — *Thelebolus* is that guild's dominant member — as do the two grey "no assignment" bands.

Read down a column and the two descriptions line up: the summer samples that are almost entirely dung saprotrophs in (B) are the samples dominated end-to-end by *Thelebolus*, *Sporormiella* and *Coniochaeta* in (A), while winter samples are a patchwork of many low-abundance genera sitting under a large unassigned fraction. The seasonal contrast is therefore the same result seen taxonomically and functionally: dung saprotrophs rise from 13.6% of winter reads to 51.5% in summer, and the unassigned fraction falls from 51.1% to 21.0% (panel C; Section 8.2). Panel A also makes the interpretive limit visible — roughly half of a typical winter sample is reads that carry no genus at all, which is the subject of the dark-taxa analysis in Section 3.4.

```{r fig1-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full build code for Figure 1 — the source of truth for figures/main/Fig1_composition_function.{png,pdf}"

# Figure 1 -- Composition and function of the dung mycobiome.
# Canonical object alldat$nopool (52 samples). Panels A and B share one sample
# axis; panel C tests the guild shares behind panel B.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig1-build

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(phyloseq); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})

rdata <- if (file.exists("eco_analysis.RData")) "eco_analysis.RData" else
         "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates/eco_analysis.RData"
load(rdata)
stopifnot(exists("alldat"), exists("funguild_otu"))   # funguild_otu <- 8_functional_guilds.R

out_dir <- "figures/main"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                  # headless: no X11 fallback

# ---- data ------------------------------------------------------------------
ps  <- alldat$nopool                                  # 52 samples, PCR reps summed
m   <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps)) m <- t(m)   # samples x taxa
rel <- m / rowSums(m)
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(rel) - 1) < 1e-10))

md     <- data.frame(as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
Season <- factor(c(winter = "Winter", summer = "Summer")[md$Season],
                 levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))
stopifnot(!anyNA(Season), identical(rownames(rel), rownames(m)))

strip_rank <- function(x) sub("^[a-z]__", "", x)      # "g__Sporormiella" -> "Sporormiella"
tax <- data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gen <- strip_rank(tax$Genus[match(colnames(m), rownames(tax))])
gen <- ifelse(gen %in% c("", "NA"), NA, gen)

# ---- panel A categories: top genera + Other + Unassigned -------------------
N_GENERA  <- 9                                        # see the palette note below
by_genus  <- t(rowsum(t(rel), group = ifelse(is.na(gen), ".unassigned", gen)))
named     <- setdiff(colnames(by_genus), ".unassigned")
top       <- names(sort(colMeans(by_genus[, named, drop = FALSE]),
                        decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(N_GENERA)]
tidy_gen  <- function(x) sub("_gen_Incertae_sedis", " (unclass.)", x)

GEN_LEVELS <- c(tidy_gen(top), "Other genera", "Unassigned (no genus)")
gen_cat    <- ifelse(is.na(gen), "Unassigned (no genus)",
              ifelse(gen %in% top, tidy_gen(gen), "Other genera"))
gen_share  <- t(rowsum(t(rel), group = gen_cat))[, GEN_LEVELS, drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(gen_share) - 1) < 1e-10))

# ---- panel B categories: FUNGuild guilds -----------------------------------
# Rule verbatim from 8_functional_guilds.R (itself from 10_hmsc.R), so Figure 1,
# appendix Section 8 and Section 9 classify OTUs identically.
COPRO_GENERA <- c("Sordaria","Podospora","Cercophora","Chaetomium","Schizothecium",
                  "Preussia","Delitschia","Pilobolus","Ascobolus","Saccobolus",
                  "Sporormiella","Coprinopsis","Thelebolus","Coniochaeta")
guild_str <- funguild_otu$Guild[match(colnames(m), funguild_otu$OTU_ID)]
is_copro  <- (!is.na(guild_str) & grepl("Dung Saprotroph", guild_str)) |
             (!is.na(gen)       & gen %in% COPRO_GENERA)
is_plant  <- !is_copro & !is.na(guild_str) &
             grepl("Endophyte|Plant Saprotroph|Plant Pathogen|Epiphyte", guild_str)
is_patho  <- !is_copro & !is_plant & !is.na(guild_str) & grepl("Pathogen|Parasite", guild_str)

GUILD_LEVELS <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
                  "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
guild_cat <- ifelse(is_copro, "Dung saprotroph",
             ifelse(is_plant, "Plant-associated",
             ifelse(is_patho, "Pathotroph",
             ifelse(!is.na(guild_str), "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark"))))
guild_share <- t(rowsum(t(rel), group = guild_cat))[, GUILD_LEVELS, drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(guild_share) - 1) < 1e-10))

# ---- shared sample order: descending dung-saprotroph share within season ----
ord <- rownames(rel)[order(Season, -guild_share[, "Dung saprotroph"])]

to_long <- function(mat, levels) data.frame(
  SampleID = factor(rep(rownames(mat), times = ncol(mat)), levels = ord),
  Season   = rep(Season, times = ncol(mat)),
  Category = factor(rep(colnames(mat), each = nrow(mat)), levels = levels),
  share    = as.vector(mat), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
genL <- to_long(gen_share, GEN_LEVELS); guiL <- to_long(guild_share, GUILD_LEVELS)
stopifnot(identical(levels(genL$SampleID), levels(guiL$SampleID)))

# ---- palettes --------------------------------------------------------------
# Guilds and Season keep the repo's Okabe-Ito assignments (8_functional_guilds.R).
# The genus scale is a separate colourblind-checked set, validated on ALL pairs
# (worst CVD dE 7.4, worst normal-vision dE 15.6) -- which is why nine genera and
# not more: a tenth hue pushes the normal-vision floor below the readable
# threshold. The thin white segment borders supply the secondary encoding that a
# CVD dE in the 6-8 band requires. Thelebolus deliberately reuses the
# dung-saprotroph orange -- it IS panel B's dominant dung saprotroph -- and grey
# #999999 likewise carries "no assignment" in both panels.
genus_cols <- setNames(
  c("#E69F00", "#8C3800", "#F0E442", "#228833", "#66CCEE",
    "#4B0055", "#AA4499", "#003D30", "#FFAABB", "#EEEEEE", "#999999"), GEN_LEVELS)
guild_cols <- c("Dung saprotroph" = "#E69F00", "Plant-associated" = "#009E73",
                "Pathotroph" = "#CC79A7", "Other assigned" = "#56B4E9",
                "Unassigned / dark" = "#999999")
season_cols <- c(Winter = "#0072B2", Summer = "#D55E00")

italicise <- function(x) ifelse(grepl("unclass\\.|^Other |^Unassigned", x), x,
                                paste0("*", x, "*"))
base_theme <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.tag         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.8, "lines"),
        legend.key.size  = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title     = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text      = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 9))
n_lab <- setNames(paste0(levels(Season), " (n = ", table(Season), ")"), levels(Season))

stacked <- function(dat, cols, title, labels = names(cols)) {
  ggplot(dat, aes(SampleID, share, fill = Category)) +
    geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.12,
             position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    facet_grid(~ Season, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x",
               labeller = labeller(Season = n_lab)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = cols, labels = labels, name = title) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    base_theme +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
}

# ---- panels A and B --------------------------------------------------------
pA <- stacked(genL, genus_cols, "Genus", italicise(GEN_LEVELS)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Read share") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1, order = 1))
# B repeats A's sample axis exactly, so its facet strips are dropped as redundant.
pB <- stacked(guiL, guild_cols, "Functional guild") +
  labs(x = "Dung sample (ordered within season by dung-saprotroph share)",
       y = "Read share") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1, order = 2)) +
  theme(strip.text = element_blank())

# ---- panel C: guild read share by season, BH-adjusted Wilcoxon -------------
season_stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(GUILD_LEVELS, function(g) {
  wt <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(guild_share[Season == "Summer", g],
                                     guild_share[Season == "Winter", g]))
  data.frame(Guild = g, p_value = wt$p.value, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
season_stats$q_value <- p.adjust(season_stats$p_value, method = "BH")
sig_lab <- function(q) ifelse(q < 0.001, "***", ifelse(q < 0.01, "**",
                       ifelse(q < 0.05, "*", "ns")))
ann <- data.frame(Category = factor(GUILD_LEVELS, levels = GUILD_LEVELS),
                  y = 1.04, lab = sig_lab(season_stats$q_value))
wrap_lab <- setNames(c("Dung\nsaprotroph", "Plant-\nassociated", "Pathotroph",
                       "Other\nassigned", "Unassigned\n/ dark"), GUILD_LEVELS)

pC <- ggplot(guiL, aes(Category, share, fill = Season)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.65, alpha = 0.85,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.12, dodge.width = 0.75),
             size = 0.9, alpha = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = ann, aes(Category, y, label = lab), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols, name = "Season") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = wrap_lab) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.09),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Per-sample read share") +
  base_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1, order = 3))

# ---- assemble and write ----------------------------------------------------
fig1 <- (pA / pB / pC) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1, 1.15), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.justification = "top")

# Every main figure is written three ways: PNG and JPG (600 dpi raster, for
# submission systems that demand one or the other) and PDF (vector, for print).
save_fig <- function(stem, obj, width, height, res = 600) {
  one <- function(open_dev) { open_dev(); on.exit(grDevices::dev.off()); print(obj) }
  one(function() grDevices::png(paste0(stem, ".png"), width = width, height = height,
                                units = "in", res = res))
  one(function() grDevices::jpeg(paste0(stem, ".jpg"), width = width, height = height,
                                 units = "in", res = res, quality = 95))
  pdf_dev <- if (capabilities("cairo")) grDevices::cairo_pdf else grDevices::pdf
  one(function() pdf_dev(paste0(stem, ".pdf"), width = width, height = height))
}
save_fig(file.path(out_dir, "Fig1_composition_function"), fig1, 10, 11)

cat(sprintf("Top %d genera (mean per-sample read share, %%):\n", N_GENERA))
print(round(100 * colMeans(gen_share), 2))
cat("\nGuild read share by season (mean %) and BH q:\n")
print(data.frame(Guild  = GUILD_LEVELS,
                 summer = round(100 * colMeans(guild_share[Season == "Summer", ]), 1),
                 winter = round(100 * colMeans(guild_share[Season == "Winter", ]), 1),
                 q      = signif(season_stats$q_value, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
```

### 10.2 Figure 2 — Seasonal turnover and its year-to-year variation (H1)

*Provenance: Fig. 2A is the ordination of Section 4.1; Fig. 2B the distance-to-Season-centroid model of Section 4.3. Test statistics are read from the committed `tables/report_permanova.csv` and `tables/report_centroid_lm.csv`, so the figure cannot drift from Section 4.*

![](figures/main/Fig2_seasonal_turnover.png)

**Figure 2**: Winter and summer dung mycobiomes differ in composition, and the size of that difference varies among years. **(A)** Unconstrained principal coordinates analysis of robust Aitchison distances among the 52 canonical samples, coloured by season and shaped by year. Thin lines join each sample to its season centroid (×). **(B)** Distance of each sample to its own season centroid in robust-CLR space, split by season and year; boxes show the median and interquartile range and points are individual samples. Subtitles give the PERMANOVA terms (A) and the ANOVA terms of the `distance ~ Season × Year` model of within-season spread (B).

Winter and summer communities separate along the first ordination axis: Season explains 11% of compositional variance (PERMANOVA p = 0.002; Table S5). The seasonal contrast is not, however, of constant size — the Season × Year interaction is significant (R² = 0.10, p = 0.011), and the per-year tests in Table S5b place almost all of the separation in 2023 (R² = 0.24, p = 0.005) with 2022 showing essentially none (R² = 0.02, p = 0.789 — a figure that is itself sensitive to the distance measure, see Section 4.2 caveat iii). Panel B shows that this is a difference in *where* the seasons sit rather than in how tightly each clusters: summer samples are consistently further from their own centroid than winter samples in every year (Season p \< 0.001), with no Season × Year interaction in that spread (p = 0.79). Two caveats belong with this figure and are treated in Section 4.2: summer samples are significantly more dispersed than winter ones, so part of the PERMANOVA R² reflects spread rather than location alone (Anderson 2001), and the axis percentages are inflated because `vegan`'s robust Aitchison distance is built from a rank-3 completion of the robust CLR matrix, so panel A plots two of only three available dimensions (Section 4.1).

```{r fig2-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full build code for Figure 2 — the source of truth for figures/main/Fig2_seasonal_turnover.{png,jpg,pdf}"

# Figure 2 -- Seasonal turnover and its year-to-year variation (H1).
# Both panels reuse the Section 4 analysis verbatim (working/report_prep_permanova.R):
# panel A the unconstrained robust-Aitchison PCoA, panel B the distance-to-
# Season-centroid in rCLR space. Test statistics are READ from the committed
# tables/ CSVs so the figure and Section 4 can never drift apart.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig2-build

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(phyloseq); library(vegan); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})

rdata <- if (file.exists("eco_analysis.RData")) "eco_analysis.RData" else
         "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates/eco_analysis.RData"
load(rdata)
tab_dir <- if (dir.exists("tables")) "tables" else
           "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/Scripts_server/Supplementary/tables"
out_dir <- "figures/main"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                  # headless: no X11 fallback

season_cols <- c(Winter = "#0072B2", Summer = "#D55E00")   # repo standard
# Fillable shapes (21/24/22, not 16/17/15) so BOTH panels map Season to `fill`
# and the two panels can share one Season key.
year_shapes <- c(`2022` = 21, `2023` = 24, `2024` = 22)
base_theme  <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.tag        = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
        legend.key.size = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title    = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text     = element_text(size = 9))

# ---- data ------------------------------------------------------------------
ps      <- alldat$nopool                              # canonical, 52 samples
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)
meta    <- data.frame(sample_data(ps), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(otu_mat), rownames(meta)))
Season  <- factor(c(winter = "Winter", summer = "Summer")[meta$Season],
                  levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))
Year    <- factor(meta$Year)
stopifnot(!anyNA(Season), !anyNA(Year))

# ---- panel A: unconstrained PCoA on robust Aitchison distances -------------
d_ait <- vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison")
attr(d_ait, "Labels") <- rownames(otu_mat)   # vegdist drops Labels for robust.aitchison
ord   <- capscale(d_ait ~ 1)
# Defensive only: this distance yields exactly 3 positive eigenvalues and no
# negative ones, because vegan's rclr completes the matrix at rank 3 (Section 4.1).
eig   <- pmax(ord$CA$eig, 0)
ax1p  <- round(100 * eig[1] / sum(eig), 1); ax2p <- round(100 * eig[2] / sum(eig), 1)

sc <- as.data.frame(scores(ord, display = "sites", choices = 1:2, scaling = 1))
colnames(sc)[1:2] <- c("Axis1", "Axis2")
sc$Season <- Season[match(rownames(sc), rownames(meta))]
sc$Year   <- Year[match(rownames(sc), rownames(meta))]
cent <- aggregate(cbind(Axis1, Axis2) ~ Season, data = sc, FUN = mean)
names(cent) <- c("Season", "cX", "cY")
sc <- merge(sc, cent, by = "Season")

perm <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
pr   <- perm[perm$term == "Season", ]
pi   <- perm[perm$term == "Season:Year", ]
by_y <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova_by_year.csv"), check.names = FALSE)

pA <- ggplot(sc, aes(Axis1, Axis2)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = cX, yend = cY, colour = Season),
               alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Season, shape = Year), size = 2.8,
             colour = "grey25", stroke = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = cent, aes(cX, cY, colour = Season), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 4.5, shape = 4, stroke = 1.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = year_shapes) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = paste0("PCoA1 (", ax1p, "%)"), y = paste0("PCoA2 (", ax2p, "%)"),
       subtitle = sprintf("PERMANOVA  Season: R² = %.2f, p = %.3f\nSeason × Year: R² = %.2f, p = %.3f",
                          pr$R2, pr$`Pr(>F)`, pi$R2, pi$`Pr(>F)`)) +
  base_theme +
  guides(fill  = guide_legend(order = 1, override.aes = list(shape = 21, size = 3)),
         shape = guide_legend(order = 2, override.aes = list(fill = "grey45", size = 3)))

# ---- panel B: distance to Season centroid, by Season x Year ----------------
rclr <- decostand(otu_mat, "rclr", MARGIN = 1)
dimnames(rclr) <- dimnames(otu_mat)          # vegan's rclr path drops dimnames
centroids <- rowsum(rclr, group = meta$Season) / as.vector(table(meta$Season))
euclid <- function(x, y) sqrt(sum((x - y)^2))
dcent <- data.frame(
  Season = Season, Year = Year,
  dist   = vapply(seq_len(nrow(rclr)),
                  function(k) euclid(rclr[k, ], centroids[meta$Season[k], ]), numeric(1)))

lmres <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_centroid_lm.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
pfmt  <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else sprintf("p = %.2f", p)
p_sea <- lmres$`Pr(>F)`[lmres$term == "Season"]
p_int <- lmres$`Pr(>F)`[lmres$term == "Season:Year"]

pB <- ggplot(dcent, aes(Year, dist, fill = Season)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.65, alpha = 0.85,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.75),
             size = 1.3, alpha = 0.7, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Distance to season centroid (rCLR)",
       subtitle = sprintf("Within-season spread\nSeason: %s;  Season × Year: %s",
                          pfmt(p_sea), pfmt(p_int))) +
  base_theme +
  # Panel A already carries the Season key; a second one would not merge with it
  # (different key glyph) and would just be printed twice.
  guides(fill = "none")

# ---- assemble and write ----------------------------------------------------
fig2 <- (pA | pB) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1.25, 1), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal")

# Every main figure is written three ways: PNG and JPG (600 dpi raster, for
# submission systems that demand one or the other) and PDF (vector, for print).
save_fig <- function(stem, obj, width, height, res = 600) {
  one <- function(open_dev) { open_dev(); on.exit(grDevices::dev.off()); print(obj) }
  one(function() grDevices::png(paste0(stem, ".png"), width = width, height = height,
                                units = "in", res = res))
  one(function() grDevices::jpeg(paste0(stem, ".jpg"), width = width, height = height,
                                 units = "in", res = res, quality = 95))
  pdf_dev <- if (capabilities("cairo")) grDevices::cairo_pdf else grDevices::pdf
  one(function() pdf_dev(paste0(stem, ".pdf"), width = width, height = height))
}
save_fig(file.path(out_dir, "Fig2_seasonal_turnover"), fig2, 10, 5.4)

cat(sprintf("PCoA axes: %.1f%% / %.1f%%\n", ax1p, ax2p))
cat(sprintf("PERMANOVA Season R2 = %.3f, p = %.3f\n", pr$R2, pr$`Pr(>F)`))
cat("Mean distance to season centroid:\n")
print(round(tapply(dcent$dist, list(dcent$Season, dcent$Year), mean), 1))
```

### 10.3 Figure 3 — Richness rises, evenness collapses (H2)

*Provenance: Fig. 3A is the coverage-based iNEXT3D analysis of Section 5.1 (Table S8); Fig. 3B the per-sample Hill numbers of Section 5.2 (Figure S8), annotated with the mixed-model contrasts of Table S9; Fig. 3C the dominance and evenness metrics of Section 5.3 (Table S10); Fig. 3D the top-5 dominant OTUs of Section 5.4 (Table S11), coloured by the guild rule of Section 8.1. Panels B–D are computed on the canonical 52-sample object (`alldat$nopool`, rarefied for B); panel A's estimates and every test statistic are read from the committed `tables/` CSVs, so the figure cannot drift from Section 5.*

![](figures/main/Fig3_richness_evenness_crossover.png)

**Figure 3**: Summer dung mycobiomes hold more fungal OTUs than winter ones, yet each individual dropping is far less even. **(A)** Asymptotic taxonomic diversity of each season's pooled sample set (iNEXT3D, incidence data, 500 bootstraps) at Hill orders q = 0, 1 and 2; points are the asymptotic estimate, bars are 95% confidence intervals, and the grey segment joins the two seasons within an order. Summer exceeds winter at every order, with no pair of intervals overlapping. **(B)** Per-sample Hill numbers for the same 52 samples, rarefied to a common depth of 12,615 reads, drawn in the same three columns against the same season axis so that the two rows can be read against one another; boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, white diamonds are season means, and the grey segment joins those means. The slope that rises in all three columns of (A) rises only at q = 0 here and falls at q = 1 and q = 2 — that reversal is the crossover. Annotations give the season contrast (summer minus winter) with its p-value from the mixed models of Table S9, which are fitted at the **PCR-replicate level (n = 98)** whereas the plotted points are per-sample (n = 52) — the same pairing used for Figure S8 and Table S9 in Section 5.2. Both rows scale y freely within each column, because the three Hill orders differ by an order of magnitude. **(C)** The mechanism: per-sample top-1-OTU read share and Pielou evenness *J*, both on a 0–1 scale, with symbols as in (B) and brackets giving the Wilcoxon rank-sum result (Table S10). **(D)** The identity of the dominants — the five OTUs with the highest mean within-season read share in each season, coloured by functional guild under the rule of Section 8.1. Bar labels give that mean share and, in parentheses, the number of the season's 26 samples in which the OTU was detected at all. Taxa are named at the finest confidently assigned rank, so an OTU with no genus appears under its family, or as *unclassified* plus its order or class. *Candida parapsilosis* is coloured plant-associated because its compound FUNGuild string contains `Epiphyte`; the rule is applied unchanged rather than special-cased, so that Figures 1 and 3 and Sections 8–10 classify every OTU identically.

Panels A and B put the same question to two scales and get opposite answers, and that disagreement is the result rather than a problem with it. Pooled across a season, summer is the richer assemblage at every Hill order — an estimated 1,708 OTUs against winter's 1,046 at q = 0, and the gap survives abundance weighting (978 vs 493 at q = 1; 523 vs 209 at q = 2) with no overlapping confidence intervals. Within a single dropping the ordering reverses as soon as abundance enters: summer leads at q = 0 (47.7 vs 31.1 effective OTUs; +18.8 in the replicate-level model, p = 0.011) but falls behind at q = 1 (7.4 vs 14.9) and significantly so at q = 2 (4.6 vs 10.1; −3.9, p = 0.010). Panel C locates the reversal in dominance rather than in the species lists: an average summer sample gives 56% of its reads to a single OTU against 25% in winter, and Pielou evenness falls from 0.72 to 0.38 (both p \< 0.001). Summer droppings are simultaneously longer-tailed and far more top-heavy, which is precisely the combination that lifts q = 0 while depressing q = 1 and q = 2. Panel D names the taxa responsible, and they are the ones a coprophilous account predicts: *Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta* and *Sporormiella intermedia* together take 44% of summer reads and are all dung saprotrophs, whereas winter's leading OTUs are mostly unclassified below class and carry no guild call at all — among them OTU1369, an unclassified Dothideomycete that is winter's most abundant OTU and is present in 20 of 26 winter samples, and which is taken up as a dark taxon in Section 3.4. Two caveats travel with the figure. The contrasts annotating (B) are fitted at the PCR-replicate level while the points are per-sample, so they test the same seasonal effect on the nested replicate data rather than on the plotted values themselves (Section 5.2). And the shares in (D) are seasonal averages, not universals — *Thelebolus* reaches its 24.9% mean while being detected in only 15 of the 26 summer droppings.

```{r fig3-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full build code for Figure 3 — the source of truth for figures/main/Fig3_richness_evenness_crossover.{png,jpg,pdf}"

# Figure 3 -- Richness rises, evenness collapses (H2).
# Panels A and B share one grammar (Season on x, diversity on y, faceted by Hill
# order) and one set of facet strips, so the crossover is a single visual event:
# the same three columns, with the Winter->Summer slope flipping between rows.
# C then gives the mechanism (dominance) and D the identity of the dominants.
# Per-sample quantities are recomputed from the canonical objects (Fig. 1
# precedent); every pooled estimate and test statistic is READ from a committed
# tables/ CSV (Fig. 2 precedent), with guards asserting the two agree.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig3-build

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(phyloseq); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})

rdata <- if (file.exists("eco_analysis.RData")) "eco_analysis.RData" else
         "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates/eco_analysis.RData"
load(rdata)
stopifnot(exists("alldat"), exists("alldat.rfy"), exists("alldat_full"),
          exists("funguild_otu"))                 # funguild_otu <- 8_functional_guilds.R
tab_dir <- if (dir.exists("tables")) "tables" else
           "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/Scripts_server/Supplementary/tables"
out_dir <- "figures/main"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                 # headless: no X11 fallback

# ---- shared style ----------------------------------------------------------
# Season and guild palettes are the repo standard (8_functional_guilds.R), so one
# colour means one thing across Fig. 1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 3.
season_cols  <- c(Winter = "#0072B2", Summer = "#D55E00")
guild_cols   <- c("Dung saprotroph" = "#E69F00", "Plant-associated" = "#009E73",
                  "Pathotroph" = "#CC79A7", "Other assigned" = "#56B4E9",
                  "Unassigned / dark" = "#999999")
GUILD_LEVELS <- names(guild_cols)

# The one facet vocabulary shared by panels A and B. A carries the strips; B
# repeats the columns beneath it and blanks them, exactly as Fig. 1B does.
Q_LEVELS <- c("q = 0  (richness)", "q = 1  (Shannon)", "q = 2  (Simpson)")

base_theme <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.tag         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.8, "lines"),
        legend.key.size  = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title     = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text      = element_text(size = 9))

# All in-plot text is ASCII. save_fig() falls back to grDevices::pdf when cairo
# is unavailable, and that device silently substitutes a dot for a Unicode minus
# or delta -- a corrupted PDF that would not fail the build.
pfmt <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "p = NA",
                    ifelse(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", sprintf("p = %.3f", p)))
to_season <- function(x) factor(c(winter = "Winter", summer = "Summer")[as.character(x)],
                                levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))

# ============================================================================
# Panel A -- season-pool diversity (Section 5.1, Table S8)
# ============================================================================
# Read, never recomputed: iNEXT3D with nboot = 500 is expensive and its estimates
# are already committed. Pooling samples within a Season asks about the Season's
# whole species pool, which is the question q0/q1/q2 answer in the same direction.
asy <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "H2_iNEXT3D_TD_asymptotic.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
qmap <- setNames(Q_LEVELS, c("Species richness", "Shannon diversity", "Simpson diversity"))
stopifnot(all(asy$qTD %in% names(qmap)), setequal(asy$Assemblage, c("Summer", "Winter")))
asy$q      <- factor(unname(qmap[asy$qTD]), levels = Q_LEVELS)
asy$Season <- factor(asy$Assemblage, levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))

pick  <- function(sea) { d <- asy[asy$Season == sea, ]
                         d[match(Q_LEVELS, as.character(d$q)), ] }
A_sum <- pick("Summer"); A_win <- pick("Winter")
# The panel's whole claim in one line: summer above winter at every order, with
# 95% CIs that do not overlap. If that ever stops being true, the build stops.
stopifnot(all(A_sum$qTD.LCL > A_win$qTD.UCL))

pA <- ggplot(asy, aes(Season, TD_asy)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = qTD.LCL, ymax = qTD.UCL, colour = Season),
                width = 0.12, linewidth = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Season), shape = 21, size = 3.4,
             colour = "grey25", stroke = 0.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ q, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.18, 0.18))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Season pool\n(effective no. of OTUs)",
       subtitle = "Asymptotic diversity of the pooled season (iNEXT3D, incidence, 500 bootstraps); bars are 95% CIs.\nSummer exceeds winter at every order, and no pair of intervals overlaps.") +
  base_theme +
  # A's x axis is identical to B's directly below, so only B prints it.
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) +
  guides(fill = "none", colour = "none")

# ============================================================================
# Panel B -- per-sample diversity (Section 5.2, Fig. S9 + Table S9)
# ============================================================================
# alldat.rfy$nopool is ALREADY rarefied to a common depth, so hill_taxa() here is
# deterministic and no seed is involved; the guard makes that testable.
ps_rfy <- alldat.rfy$nopool
m_rfy  <- as(otu_table(ps_rfy), "matrix")
if (taxa_are_rows(ps_rfy)) m_rfy <- t(m_rfy)         # hillR wants sites x species
stopifnot(nsamples(ps_rfy) == 52L, length(unique(rowSums(m_rfy))) == 1L)
rfy_depth <- unique(rowSums(m_rfy))

md_rfy <- data.frame(as(sample_data(ps_rfy), "data.frame"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(m_rfy), rownames(md_rfy)))
season_rfy <- to_season(md_rfy$Season); stopifnot(!anyNA(season_rfy))

hill <- data.frame(Season = season_rfy,
                   q0 = hillR::hill_taxa(m_rfy, q = 0),
                   q1 = hillR::hill_taxa(m_rfy, q = 1),
                   q2 = hillR::hill_taxa(m_rfy, q = 2))
hill_long <- data.frame(
  Season = rep(hill$Season, times = 3),
  q      = factor(rep(Q_LEVELS, each = nrow(hill)), levels = Q_LEVELS),
  value  = c(hill$q0, hill$q1, hill$q2))

# IMPORTANT -- the two levels differ, deliberately. The points are PER SAMPLE
# (n = 52, PCR replicates summed); the annotated contrast is the mixed model of
# Table S9, fitted at the PCR-REPLICATE level because that is where the replicate
# random intercept is estimable. Section 5.2 pairs Fig. S9 and Table S9 the same
# way and the caption says so. The guard is the safety net: if the two levels
# ever stopped telling the same story, their season differences would disagree
# in sign and the build would stop.
n_pcr <- sum(sample_sums(alldat_full[[1]]) >= 10000)   # Section 5.2 depth filter,
                                                       # reproduced without refitting
lmm <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "H2_lmm_season_effect.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(setequal(lmm$metric, c("q0", "q1", "q2")))
lmm <- lmm[match(c("q0", "q1", "q2"), lmm$metric), ]
obs_diff <- vapply(c("q0", "q1", "q2"), function(q)
  mean(hill[[q]][hill$Season == "Summer"]) - mean(hill[[q]][hill$Season == "Winter"]),
  numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(sign(obs_diff) == sign(lmm$summer_minus_winter)))

# Boxes show medians, but Section 5.3's text quotes MEANS -- so the means are
# drawn, and the segment joining them is what makes the slope flip legible
# against panel A directly above.
meanB <- aggregate(value ~ q + Season, hill_long, mean)
y_top <- as.numeric(tapply(hill_long$value, hill_long$q, max)[Q_LEVELS])
ann_B <- data.frame(q     = factor(Q_LEVELS, levels = Q_LEVELS),
                    value = y_top * 1.32,
                    lab   = sprintf("summer - winter\n%+.1f, %s",
                                    lmm$summer_minus_winter, pfmt(lmm$p)))

# seed = on the jitter: save_fig() prints the object once per device, and an
# unseeded jitter would place the points differently in the PNG, the JPG and the
# PDF -- three subtly different figures from one build.
pB <- ggplot(hill_long, aes(Season, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Season), outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.14, height = 0, seed = 1),
             size = 1.1, alpha = 0.55, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_line(data = meanB, aes(group = 1), colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = meanB, shape = 23, size = 2.4, stroke = 0.5,
             fill = "white", colour = "grey15") +
  geom_text(data = ann_B, aes(x = 1.5, label = lab), inherit.aes = TRUE,
            size = 2.9, lineheight = 0.95, vjust = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ q, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  # Linear, not log: a Hill number is an effective number of OTUs and is meant to
  # be read off the axis. free_y absorbs the 164-vs-32 range difference instead.
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.04, 0.36))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Per sample\n(effective no. of OTUs)",
       subtitle = sprintf("Per-sample Hill numbers (n = %d, rarefied to %s reads); white diamonds are season means.\nAnnotations: PCR-replicate-level mixed model (n = %d; Table S9).",
                          nrow(hill), format(rfy_depth, big.mark = ","), n_pcr)) +
  base_theme +
  # B repeats A's facet columns exactly, so its strips are dropped as redundant.
  theme(strip.text = element_blank()) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(order = 1))

# ============================================================================
# Panel C -- dominance and evenness, the mechanism (Section 5.3, Table S10)
# ============================================================================
ps  <- alldat$nopool                                 # canonical, raw counts
m   <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix")
if (!taxa_are_rows(ps)) m <- t(m)                    # taxa x samples, as 5.3 uses
rel <- sweep(m, 2, colSums(m), "/")
stopifnot(all(abs(colSums(rel) - 1) < 1e-10))
md  <- data.frame(as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(rel), rownames(md)),
          setequal(colnames(rel), rownames(m_rfy)))  # B and C/D are the same 52 birds
season_c <- to_season(md$Season)

pielou_J <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; -sum(p * log(p)) / log(length(p)) }
dom <- data.frame(Season    = season_c,
                  top1_prop = apply(rel, 2, max),
                  pielou_J  = apply(rel, 2, pielou_J))

# Drift guard: the recomputed means must reproduce committed Table S10 exactly at
# the precision the CSV stores (1 dp for the percentage, 2 dp for J).
dom_csv <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_dominance_summary.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
dom_csv <- dom_csv[match(c("winter", "summer"), dom_csv$Season), ]
obs_top1 <- tapply(dom$top1_prop, dom$Season, mean)
obs_J    <- tapply(dom$pielou_J,  dom$Season, mean)
stopifnot(max(abs(round(100 * as.numeric(obs_top1[c("Winter","Summer")]), 1) -
                  dom_csv$mean_top1_prop_pct)) < 1e-8,
          max(abs(round(as.numeric(obs_J[c("Winter","Summer")]), 2) -
                  dom_csv$mean_pielou_J)) < 1e-8)
p_top1 <- unique(dom_csv$wilcox_p_top1_prop); p_J <- unique(dom_csv$wilcox_p_pielou_J)
stopifnot(length(p_top1) == 1L, length(p_J) == 1L)

# Both metrics live on 0-1, so one shared axis works and the mechanism reads as a
# single picture: the seasons swap sides between the two metric groups.
# <br> not \n: these labels are rendered by element_markdown, which honours HTML
# breaks. Wrapped because the two names collide at this panel's width.
M_LEVELS <- c("Top-1 OTU<br>read share", "Pielou<br>evenness *J*")
dom_long <- data.frame(
  Season = rep(dom$Season, times = 2),
  Metric = factor(rep(M_LEVELS, each = nrow(dom)), levels = M_LEVELS),
  value  = c(dom$top1_prop, dom$pielou_J))
meanC <- aggregate(value ~ Metric + Season, dom_long, mean)
brk   <- data.frame(Metric = factor(M_LEVELS, levels = M_LEVELS),
                    lab    = pfmt(c(p_top1, p_J)),
                    xmid   = seq_along(M_LEVELS))
brk$xmin <- brk$xmid - 0.19; brk$xmax <- brk$xmid + 0.19  # dodge(0.75) box centres

pC <- ggplot(dom_long, aes(Metric, value, fill = Season)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.65, alpha = 0.85,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.12, dodge.width = 0.75,
                                             seed = 1),
             size = 1.1, alpha = 0.55, colour = "grey20", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = meanC, aes(group = Season), inherit.aes = TRUE,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), shape = 23, size = 2.3,
             stroke = 0.5, fill = "white", colour = "grey15", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_segment(data = brk, aes(x = xmin, xend = xmax, y = 1.03, yend = 1.03),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = brk, aes(x = xmid, y = 1.055, label = lab), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3, vjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.13), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Per-sample value (proportion)",
       subtitle = "White diamonds are season means;\nbrackets give the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Table S10).") +
  base_theme +
  # The x labels carry markdown (*J*); without element_markdown the asterisks
  # print literally, and this theme() must come after base_theme to win.
  theme(axis.text.x = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 9)) +
  guides(fill = "none")

# ============================================================================
# Panel D -- who the dominants are (Section 5.4, Table S11), by guild
# ============================================================================
top5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(season_c), function(s) {
  cols   <- colnames(rel)[season_c == s]
  shares <- rowMeans(rel[, cols, drop = FALSE])      # mean WITHIN-season share
  ids    <- names(sort(shares, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
  data.frame(Season = s, OTU = ids, share = 100 * shares[ids],
             n_detect = rowSums(rel[ids, cols, drop = FALSE] > 0),
             n_season = length(cols), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
top5$Season <- factor(top5$Season, levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))

# Drift guard: same OTUs, same order, same shares as committed Table S11.
t5_csv <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_top5_otu_by_season.csv"),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
t5_csv$Season <- to_season(t5_csv$Season)
t5_csv <- t5_csv[order(t5_csv$Season, -t5_csv$mean_pct_share), ]
chk    <- top5[order(top5$Season, -top5$share), ]
stopifnot(identical(paste(chk$Season, chk$OTU), paste(t5_csv$Season, t5_csv$OTU)),
          max(abs(round(chk$share, 2) - t5_csv$mean_pct_share)) < 1e-8)

# UNITE taxonomy carries rank prefixes ("g__Thelebolus") and, at species level, a
# trailing hypothesis index ("intermedia 1"). Labels fall back down the ranks
# until something is assigned: a family name stands alone unambiguously, an order
# or class does not and is prefixed "unclassified". Markdown asterisks italicise
# real Latin names only -- never a rank name, never an Incertae sedis placeholder.
tax <- data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
strip_rank <- function(x) sub("^[a-z]__", "", x)
clean_rank <- function(x) { x <- strip_rank(x)
  x[is.na(x) | x == "" | x == "NA" | grepl("unidentified", x, ignore.case = TRUE)] <- NA_character_
  x }
otu_label <- function(otu) {
  rk <- lapply(c("Genus", "Species", "Family", "Order", "Class"),
               function(r) clean_rank(tax[otu, r]))
  names(rk) <- c("Genus", "Species", "Family", "Order", "Class")
  incertae <- function(x) !is.na(x) && grepl("Incertae_sedis", x)
  nm <-
    if (!is.na(rk$Genus) && !incertae(rk$Genus)) {
      if (!is.na(rk$Species))
        paste0("*", rk$Genus, " ", sub("[ _]+[0-9]+$", "", rk$Species), "*")
      else paste0("*", rk$Genus, "*")
    } else if (incertae(rk$Genus))                      sub("_gen_Incertae_sedis", " (unclass.)", rk$Genus)
      else if (!is.na(rk$Family) && !incertae(rk$Family)) rk$Family
      else if (!is.na(rk$Order))                        paste("unclassified", rk$Order)
      else if (!is.na(rk$Class))                        paste("unclassified", rk$Class)
      else                                              "unclassified fungus"
  paste0(nm, " (", otu, ")")
}
top5$label <- unname(vapply(top5$OTU, otu_label, character(1)))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(top5$label))

# Guild rule VERBATIM from the Fig. 1 chunk (itself from 8_functional_guilds.R),
# including its genus cleaning, so Fig. 1, Fig. 3, Section 8 and Section 9 all
# classify an OTU identically. One consequence is visible here: FUNGuild returns
# a compound string for Candida parapsilosis containing "Epiphyte", so the
# priority rule lands OTU136 in Plant-associated. That is an artifact of compound
# FUNGuild strings, not a claim about the taxon -- but the rule is applied
```
